children.translated_text: Chapter 1
<s>Oṃ</s> — Homage to the <s>Buddha</s>.
Having bowed with devotion to the <s>Sugatas</s> together with their sons, with the body of the <s>Dharma</s>,
and to all who are worthy of veneration,
I shall describe the entry into the vow of the sons of the <s>Sugatas</s>,
in accordance with scripture, in brief.
There is nothing here that has not been said before,
nor do I have any skill in composition.
Therefore I have no thought for the benefit of others;
this is composed to cultivate my own mind.
By this, first of all, the force of my devotion
to cultivating what is wholesome increases.
And if another of a nature similar to mine should see this,
then this too would be meaningful.
This fortunate moment is extremely difficult to obtain
and, once obtained, accomplishes the purpose of a human being.
If one does not reflect upon what is beneficial here,
how will this conjunction come again?
Just as on a night of dense, dark clouds
lightning for an instant reveals a flash of brightness,
so by the power of the <s>Buddhas</s>, sometimes,
the mind of the world turns toward merit, if only for a moment.
Therefore, what is wholesome is always feeble,
while the power of evil is great and exceedingly terrible.
By what other virtue could it be overcome,
if there were not the mind of awakening (<s>bodhicitta</s>)?
The lords of sages, contemplating through innumerable aeons,
have seen that this alone is beneficial:
for it causes an ever-growing happiness
to overflow immeasurable multitudes of beings with ease.
By those who wish to cross the hundreds of sufferings of existence,
who wish to remove the afflictions of beings,
who wish to enjoy hundreds of happinesses —
the mind of awakening (<s>bodhicitta</s>) must never be abandoned.
A wretch bound as a prisoner of <s>saṃsāra</s>
is called a son of the <s>Sugatas</s> in an instant.
He becomes worthy of veneration by the worlds of gods and humans
the moment the mind of awakening (<s>bodhicitta</s>) arises.
Taking this impure form,
it transforms it into the priceless image of the jewel of the <s>Jinas</s>.
Grasp firmly the elixir known as
the mind of awakening (<s>bodhicitta</s>), which is like the supreme alchemical substance.
Well examined by those of immeasurable wisdom,
the sole caravan-leaders of the world, [and found] of great value —
you who are accustomed to wandering through the stations of [lower] existences,
grasp firmly the jewel of the mind of awakening (<s>bodhicitta</s>).
Like the plantain tree that perishes after bearing fruit,
all other virtues indeed decay.
But the tree of the mind of awakening (<s>bodhicitta</s>) bears fruit constantly and does not decay;
it continues to produce [fruit] perpetually.
Having committed even terrible sins,
by relying on it one crosses over in an instant —
just as by relying on a hero one [crosses] great dangers.
Why then is it not resorted to by ignorant beings?
Like the fire at the end of an age, it burns up
great sins in an instant.
Its immeasurable benefits were declared
by the wise Lord <s>Maitreya</s> to <s>Sudhana</s>.
That mind of awakening (<s>bodhicitta</s>) should be understood
as being of two kinds in brief:
the mind of aspiration for awakening (<s>bodhipraṇidhicitta</s>)
and the mind of engagement in awakening (<s>bodhiprasthāna</s>).
Just as the distinction is understood
between one who wishes to go and one who goes,
so the wise should know the distinction
between these two, in that order.
The mind of aspiration for awakening (<s>bodhipraṇidhicitta</s>)
produces great fruit even in <s>saṃsāra</s>,
but not the uninterrupted [flow of] merit
as does the mind of engagement (<s>prasthānacitta</s>).
From the moment when one takes up that mind
for the liberation of the boundless realm of beings,
with an irreversible resolve —
from that time onward, even for one asleep
or heedless, in manifold ways,
uninterrupted streams of merit
flow forth, vast as the sky.
This, with supporting reasoning,
the <s>Tathāgata</s> Himself declared
in the <s>Subāhupṛcchā</s> [-sūtra]
for the sake of beings of lesser aspiration.
One who, with benevolent intention, thinks
'I shall remove the headaches of beings,'
is held [to possess]
immeasurable merit.
How much more so one who wishes to remove
the immeasurable suffering of each and every being
and wishes to bring about immeasurable virtue
for each and every being?
Whose mother or father
has such a wish for [one's] welfare?
Do the gods, or the sages,
or <s>Brahmā</s> possess it?
For those very beings, even for their own sake,
such a wish has never arisen before,
not even in a dream.
How could it arise for the sake of others?
How does this extraordinary jewel among beings arise —
unprecedented —
one whose intention for the welfare of others
does not arise in others even for their own sake?
The merit of the jewel-mind
that is the seed of joy for the world
and the medicine for the world's suffering —
how indeed can it be measured?
By the mere wish for [others'] welfare,
the worship of the <s>Buddhas</s> is surpassed.
How much more so by the effort
for the complete happiness of all beings?
They rush toward suffering itself,
with the wish to escape suffering.
Out of the very desire for happiness, through delusion,
they destroy their own happiness like an enemy.
One who would satisfy with happiness
those destitute of joy, afflicted in manifold ways,
and who would cut off all their afflictions —
and who would also destroy their delusion —
where is a virtuous one equal to him?
Where is such a friend?
Where is such merit?
Even one who returns a favor
is praised for that much.
But what shall be said of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>
who does good unsolicited?
One who gives a meal to a few people
is honored by the world as a doer of good —
for a mere gift of a moment's ordinary food,
contemptuously sustaining [them] for half a day.
What then of one who gives to a limitless number of beings,
for a limitless time,
the fulfillment of every wish,
inexhaustible until the exhaustion of all sky-dwelling beings?
One who harbors malice in his heart
toward such a lord of the feast, a son of the <s>Jinas</s>,
will dwell in the hells for as many aeons
as the number of malicious thoughts — so the Lord has said.
But one whose mind turns to faith [toward them]
produces fruit even greater than that.
For even amidst great force, evil action [toward] sons of the <s>Jinas</s>
[is surpassed by] virtue [arising] effortlessly.
I bow to the bodies of those
in whom that precious jewel-mind has arisen.
Even offense toward them leads to happiness.
I go for refuge to those sources of joy.
[End of] the first chapter, called 'The Benefits of the Mind of Awakening (<s>Bodhicitta</s>),' in the <s>Bodhicaryāvatāra</s>. ||
Chapter 2
In order to properly grasp that jewel-mind,
I make offerings to the <s>Tathāgatas</s>,
to the stainless jewel of the true <s>Dharma</s>,
and to the sons of the <s>Buddhas</s>, oceans of virtue.
Whatever flowers and fruits there are,
whatever kinds of medicinal herbs exist,
whatever gems there are in the world,
and waters that are clear and delightful,
mountains made of jewels and likewise others,
forest regions charming in their solitude,
creepers resplendent with the ornament of flowers,
and trees with branches bowed low with fine fruits,
fragrances and incenses from the worlds of gods and others,
wish-fulfilling trees and trees made of jewels,
lakes adorned with lotuses,
supremely enchanting with the calls of swans,
crops grown without cultivation,
and other ornaments worthy of offering,
as vast as the expanse of space, limitless —
all these ownerless [things],
taking them up in my mind, I offer
to the chiefs of sages together with their sons.
May those supremely worthy of gifts accept these from me,
the greatly compassionate ones, taking pity on me.
I am without merit, greatly destitute;
I have nothing else for offering.
Therefore, for my own sake, [O Lords] who think of others' welfare,
may the Lords accept this by their own power.
I give myself entirely to the <s>Jinas</s>
and to their sons, wholly and completely.
O supreme beings, accept me!
With devotion I enter into servitude to you.
Being accepted by you,
I shall work for the welfare of beings in existence without fear.
I shall transcend my former sins
and shall commit no further sin.
In those bath-houses fragrant,
with canopies shining with pearls,
with floors of brilliant, clear crystal,
with delightful pillars blazing with jewels,
with many great vessels made of precious gems
filled with fragrant water and flowers,
I bathe the <s>Tathāgatas</s>
and their sons, accompanied by song and music.
With incomparable cloths, fragrant and purified of stains,
I dry their bodies.
Then I offer them
excellent robes, well-dyed and well-perfumed.
With divine, soft, fine, and variously splendid
garments and the finest ornaments,
I adorn <s>Samantabhadra</s>, <s>Ajita</s>, <s>Mañjughoṣa</s>,
<s>Lokeśvara</s>, and the others.
With the finest perfumes, whose fragrance pervades
the entire three-thousandfold [world-system], I anoint
the bodies of all the lords of sages,
blazing with the radiance of well-refined, well-polished, well-washed gold.
With <s>mandāra</s>, blue lotus, jasmine, and the like —
with all fragrant and delightful flowers —
I worship the supremely worship-worthy lords of sages,
and with garlands of beautiful arrangement.
With clouds of incense, rich, diffuse, and delightful in fragrance,
I fumigate them.
With delicious foods and various drinks,
I present an offering of sustenance to them.
I offer jeweled lamps
set upon golden lotuses.
On floors anointed with perfume,
I scatter delightful heaps of flowers.
Those [celestial palaces], beautiful with hanging garlands of pearls and gems,
radiant, adorning the quarters of space,
cloud-like palace-pavilions, charming with songs of praise —
these too I offer to those endowed with loving-kindness.
With golden handles of beautiful form,
set with pearls and raised aloft,
I hold up for the great sages
jeweled parasols of supreme beauty.
Henceforth, may there arise
delightful clouds of offerings,
clouds of musical instruments and songs,
bringing joy to all beings.
Upon all the jewels of the true <s>Dharma</s>,
upon <s>caityas</s> and images,
may rains of flowers, gems, and the like
descend unceasingly.
Just as <s>Mañjughoṣa</s> and others
worship the <s>Jinas</s>,
so do I worship the <s>Tathāgatas</s>, the Lords,
together with their sons.
With hymns that are oceans of melodious sounds,
I praise these oceans of virtue.
May clouds of songs of praise
arise for them without fail.
With prostrations equal in number to the atoms
in all the [buddha-]fields, I bow
to the <s>Buddhas</s> of all three times, everywhere,
together with the <s>Dharma</s> and the supreme <s>Saṃgha</s>.
I venerate all <s>caityas</s>
and the abodes of <s>Bodhisattvas</s>.
I pay homage to the preceptors
and likewise bow to the venerable ascetics.
I go to the <s>Buddha</s> for refuge
until the seat of awakening.
I go to the <s>Dharma</s> for refuge
and to the assembly of <s>Bodhisattvas</s> likewise.
I beseech the perfectly awakened ones
established in all directions,
and the greatly compassionate
<s>Bodhisattvas</s>, with joined palms.
In beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s>,
in this life or in others,
whatever sin I, an animal-like being, have committed
or caused to be committed,
and whatever I have rejoiced in
through delusion, to my own destruction —
that transgression I confess,
tormented by remorse.
Whatever offense against the Three Jewels,
or against my mother and father,
or against my teachers and others, through contempt,
has been committed by me in body, speech, and mind —
whatever terrible sin has been committed
by me, a sinner defiled by many faults —
O Leaders,
all of that I confess.
How shall I escape from this?
I am constantly anxious, O Leaders.
May death not come to me soon,
while my accumulation of sin has not been exhausted.
How shall I escape from this?
Protect me swiftly!
May death not come quickly
to me whose sins are unexhausted.
This death, which does not examine
what has been done and what has not, is a treacherous slayer.
Not to be trusted by the healthy or the sick,
it is a sudden, mighty thunderbolt.
For the sake of what is dear and not dear,
sin has been committed in manifold ways.
That one must abandon everything and depart —
this was not recognized thus.
Whatever things are experienced
become mere memories.
Like things experienced in a dream, everything
that has passed is not seen again.
Those who are not dear will not remain,
and those dear to me will not remain.
I too shall not remain,
and nothing at all shall remain.
Even while I still stand here,
many dear and not dear ones have gone.
But the terrible sin committed on their account
remains standing before me.
Thus, that I am a mere visitor —
this was not considered by me.
Through delusion, attachment, and hatred,
sin has been committed in manifold ways.
Day and night, without rest,
the diminishment of life increases.
And there is no replenishment of life.
Shall I not indeed die?
Even while lying here on one's bed,
even while remaining among relatives,
the pain of the cutting of vital parts
must be endured by me alone.
When seized by the messengers of <s>Yama</s>,
what kinsman is there? What friend?
Merit alone is the refuge then,
and that I have not cultivated.
Clinging to this impermanent life,
heedless, not knowing this fear,
much sin has been accumulated
by me, O Lords.
Even one being led away today
for the mere cutting of a limb grows parched,
thirsty, with wretched gaze,
seeing the world quite differently.
How much more so when one is seized
by the terrifying-formed messengers of <s>Yama</s>,
gripped by the great fever of terror,
smeared in one's own excrement?
With anxious glances,
seeking protection in the four directions —
'Who will be a good refuge for me
from this great fear?'
Seeing the directions devoid of refuge,
one falls again into bewilderment.
What shall I do then
in that place of great terror?
This very day I go for refuge
to the mighty Lords of the world,
the Conquerors (<s>Jinas</s>), striving for the protection of the world,
who remove all fear.
And to the <s>Dharma</s> attained by them,
which destroys the fear of <s>saṃsāra</s>,
I go for refuge sincerely,
and likewise to the assembly of <s>Bodhisattvas</s>.
To <s>Samantabhadra</s> I give myself,
trembling with fear.
And again to <s>Mañjughoṣa</s>
I give myself of my own accord.
And to that Lord <s>Avalokita</s>,
who moves about overcome with compassion,
I, frightened, cry out in distress —
may he protect me, a sinner!
To the noble <s>Ākāśagarbha</s>,
and to <s>Kṣitigarbha</s>, sincerely,
and to all those of great compassion —
seeking refuge, I cry out.
At the mere sight of whom
the wicked ones flee in the four directions —
the messengers of <s>Yama</s> and the like —
to Him, the Vajra-bearer (<s>Vajrapāṇi</s>), I bow.
Having transgressed your words before,
now, upon seeing the danger,
I come to you for refuge, terrified —
destroy my fear swiftly!
Even one frightened by a passing illness
should not disregard the physician's words —
how much more so one afflicted by hundreds of diseases,
the four [root afflictions] and four more?
By even one of which
all people dwelling in <s>Jambudvīpa</s>
are destroyed, and for which no remedy
is found in any direction.
That I disregard the words
of the All-knowing Physician
who removes all afflictions —
shame on me, so utterly deluded!
I stand extremely careful
even at lesser precipices —
how much more at the precipice
of a thousand leagues, lasting ages?
'Death will not come today' —
such complacency is not fitting for me.
That time will inevitably come
when I shall be no more.
By whom has fearlessness been given to me?
And how shall I escape?
Certainly I shall cease to be —
why then is my mind at ease?
What essence remains for me
from past experiences now lost,
in attachment to which
I have transgressed the words of my teachers?
Having left this world of the living
and kinsmen and acquaintances alike,
I shall go alone to some [unknown place] —
what use to me are all these friends and foes?
This alone should be my concern,
fitting day and night, always:
From evil, suffering is certain —
how shall I escape from it?
Whatever sin has been accumulated
by me, foolish and ignorant —
whether naturally wrong
or wrong by convention —
all that I confess,
standing before the Lords,
with joined palms, fearing suffering,
bowing down again and again.
May the Guides accept
my transgression as a transgression.
This was not good, O Lords —
I shall not do it again.
Thus ends the second chapter. ||
Chapter 3
The cessation of suffering in the lower realms —
the merit made by all beings —
I rejoice in with great delight.
May the suffering ones abide in happiness!
I rejoice in the liberation
of embodied beings from the suffering of <s>saṃsāra</s>,
and I rejoice in the <s>Bodhisattva</s>-hood and <s>Buddha</s>-hood
of the Protectors.
And I rejoice in the oceans of the arising of the mind [of awakening]
of the Teachers, which bring happiness to all beings
and establish the welfare
of all beings.
With joined palms I entreat
the <s>Buddhas</s> in all directions:
May they kindle the lamp of <s>Dharma</s>
for those who fall into suffering through delusion!
And the Conquerors (<s>Jinas</s>) who wish to pass into <s>Nirvāṇa</s> —
with joined palms I beseech them:
May they remain for infinite <s>kalpas</s>!
Let not this world be blind!
Having done all this,
whatever merit I have gathered —
by that may I become
the one who allays all the suffering of all beings.
May I be the medicine for the sick,
and may I be the physician as well,
and their attendant too,
until the disease does not recur.
May I destroy the torment of hunger and thirst
with showers of food and drink.
In the intermediate <s>kalpas</s> of famine,
may I become food and drink.
And for poor beings,
may I be an inexhaustible treasure,
standing before them
in the forms of manifold provisions.
My bodies, my enjoyments,
and all my merit of the three times —
I relinquish without attachment
for the accomplishment of the welfare of all beings.
The relinquishment of all is <s>Nirvāṇa</s>,
and my mind seeks <s>Nirvāṇa</s>.
If all must be relinquished by me,
better that it be given to beings.
I have given this body
for the pleasure of all embodied beings.
Let them strike, revile,
or constantly cover it with filth.
Let them play with my body,
let them laugh and amuse themselves.
I have given my body to them —
why should I be concerned about it?
Let them make me do whatever deeds
bring them happiness.
May no harm ever come
to anyone on my account.
For those who, taking me as their object,
develop a mind of anger or pleasure,
may that very [encounter] be the cause
for the perpetual accomplishment of all their aims.
Those who slander me,
and others who do me harm,
and still others who mock me —
may all of them share in awakening.
May I be the protector of the unprotected,
the guide for travelers,
a boat, a bridge,
and a causeway for those who wish to cross.
May I be a lamp for those who seek a lamp,
a bed for those who seek a bed,
a servant for those who seek a servant —
for all embodied beings.
May I be a wish-fulfilling gem, an auspicious vase,
a <s>siddha vidyā</s> (efficacious spell), a great healing herb.
May I be a wish-fulfilling tree
and a wish-granting cow for embodied beings.
Just as the elements such as earth and the like
serve in manifold ways
the immeasurable beings
dwelling throughout the whole of space —
so may I be the sustenance
in manifold ways for the realm of beings
extending to the ends of space,
until all are freed from suffering.
Just as the <s>Bodhicitta</s> (mind of awakening)
was grasped by the <s>Sugatas</s> (Buddhas) of old,
and just as they abided
in the <s>Bodhisattva</s> training step by step —
so do I generate
<s>Bodhicitta</s> for the welfare of the world,
and so shall I train
in those trainings in due order.
Having thus wisely
grasped <s>Bodhicitta</s> with clarity,
in order to further nurture it,
one should gladden the mind thus:
'Today my birth is fruitful,
my human existence is well-obtained.
Today I am born in the family of the <s>Buddha</s>;
I am now a child of the <s>Buddha</s>.
Henceforth I must act
in a manner befitting those of my family,
so that no stain may come
upon this pure lineage.'
Just as a blind person
might find a jewel in a heap of refuse,
so too, somehow,
this <s>Bodhicitta</s> has arisen in me.
This elixir has arisen
for the destruction of death in the world.
This inexhaustible treasure
alleviates the poverty of the world.
This is the supreme medicine
that pacifies the disease of the world.
It is the tree of rest for the world,
weary from wandering on the road of existence.
It is the universal bridge
for crossing over the lower realms, for all travelers.
It is the risen moon of the mind
that cools the heat of the world's afflictions.
It is the great sun that dispels
the darkness of the world's ignorance.
It is the fresh butter arisen
from churning the milk of the true <s>Dharma</s>.
For the caravan of beings traveling
the road of existence, hungering for the enjoyment of happiness,
this feast of happiness has been prepared,
satisfying all beings who have arrived.
Today the world is invited by me
to <s>Sugata</s>-hood (Buddhahood) and happiness in the interim.
May gods, <s>Asuras</s>, and all others
rejoice in the presence of all the Protectors!
Thus ends the third chapter of the <s>Bodhicaryāvatāra</s>, entitled 'The Embrace of <s>Bodhicitta</s>.' ||
Chapter 4
Having thus firmly grasped
<s>Bodhicitta</s>, the child of the Conquerors (<s>Jinas</s>)
should strive constantly and untiringly
not to transgress the trainings.
Regarding what was undertaken hastily,
without proper deliberation —
even a vow 'I shall not do it'
is fitting there.
But that which has been examined by the <s>Buddhas</s>,
by the greatly wise and by their children,
and by me too according to my ability —
why should one hesitate in that?
And if, having vowed thus,
I do not fulfill it in action —
having deceived all these [beings],
what destiny will be mine?
It is said that even a person who,
having thought of giving in his mind, does not give,
becomes a <s>preta</s> (hungry ghost) —
even regarding a trifling thing.
How much more so if, having loudly proclaimed
the unsurpassed happiness sincerely,
I deceive the entire world —
what destiny will be mine?
Only the Omniscient One knows
the inconceivable course of <s>karma</s> —
that even those who abandon <s>Bodhicitta</s>
He still liberates.
Therefore, for a <s>Bodhisattva</s>,
every transgression is extremely grave,
for when he transgresses,
he undermines the welfare of all beings.
And anyone else who, even for a moment,
creates an obstacle to his merit —
there is no end to the lower realms for that person
who undermines the welfare of beings.
For by destroying the welfare
of even a single being, one is destroyed oneself —
how much more so [by destroying the welfare]
of beings dwelling throughout the whole of space?
Thus, tossed about in <s>saṃsāra</s>
by the force of transgression and the force of <s>Bodhicitta</s>,
one is long delayed
in attaining the [Bodhisattva] stages.
Therefore I must fulfill with care
what I have vowed.
If effort is not made today,
I have sunk from depth to depth.
Countless <s>Buddhas</s> have gone by,
seekers of all beings.
Through my own fault, I have not come
within the range of their healing.
And if today too I remain as I have been,
again and again I shall obtain
the lower realms, disease, death,
mutilation, dismemberment, and the like.
When shall I obtain — so extremely rare —
the arising of a <s>Tathāgata</s>,
faith, human birth,
and fitness for the practice of virtue?
This day of health,
with food and free from adversity —
life is but a deceptive moment,
the body like a borrowed thing.
Indeed, through such conduct of mine,
human birth will not be obtained again.
And if human birth is not obtained,
there is only sin — whence virtue?
When, though capable of virtue,
I do not practice it —
bewildered by the sufferings of the lower realms,
what shall I do then?
For one who does not practice virtue
and accumulates sin —
even the word '<s>Sugata</s>' (a good destiny) is destroyed
for hundreds of <s>koṭis</s> of <s>kalpas</s>.
Therefore the <s>Bhagavān</s> has said
that human birth is exceedingly rare —
like a turtle's neck entering the hole
of a yoke [floating] in the great ocean.
From sin committed in a single moment,
one will remain in <s>Avīci</s> for a <s>kalpa</s>.
From sin accumulated since beginningless time,
what talk is there of a good destiny?
And it is not that one is freed
having merely experienced that [suffering],
for while experiencing it,
yet further sin is generated.
There is no greater self-deception,
and no greater delusion than this:
that having obtained such a [rare] moment,
virtue was not practiced by me.
And if, having reflected thus,
I again sink down, deluded,
I shall grieve for a long time,
urged on by the messengers of <s>Yama</s>.
The unbearable fire of hell
will burn my body for a long time.
And the fire of remorse will burn
my mind for a long time — this is certain.
Having somehow reached
this exceedingly rare, beneficial ground,
even knowing [the danger], I am led
back to those very hells again.
I have no volition in this matter,
as if bewitched by spells.
I do not know by what I am deluded —
who dwells within me here?
The enemies of craving, hatred, and the like,
devoid of hands, feet, and the rest —

how then have I been enslaved by them?
Established right in my own mind,
they strike me at their ease.
And yet I do not grow angry at them —
shame on such misplaced forbearance!
Even if all gods and humans
were my enemies,
they could not lead me
into the fire of <s>Avīci</s>.
That against whose contact not even
the ashes of <s>Meru</s> would remain —
the mighty enemies, the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions),
hurl me there in an instant.
No other enemy at all
has such a long lifespan
as these, my affliction-enemies —
beginningless, endless, immensely long.
All things serve one's welfare
when attended to with friendliness;
but when these afflictions (<s>kleśas</s>) are served,
they become all the more productive of suffering.
With these perpetual, long-standing enemies,
who are the sole cause of producing floods of calamity,
dwelling in my heart fearlessly —
how can I find delight in <s>saṃsāra</s>?
These are the prison-wardens of the cycle of existence,
the executioners even in the hells and the like.
If they dwell in the cage of craving within the house of my mind,
how can there be happiness for me?
Therefore I shall not lay down this burden
until these enemies are slain before my eyes.
Those full of wrath toward even a petty offender,
swollen with pride, do not sleep until they have slain him.
Those fierce ones, eager to strike down on the battle-front
the blinded foes who are naturally subject to the suffering of death,
enduring the pain of countless arrows and spears,
do not turn away without having accomplished [their aim].
How much more so — when I am determined to destroy
the natural enemies that are the perpetual cause of all suffering:
should there be despondency and dejection in me today
for any reason, even amidst hundreds of calamities?
They bear on their bodies the wounds of enemies,
inflicted without [meaningful] cause, as if they were ornaments.
When I am striving for the supremely worthy accomplishment,
why should sufferings be obstacles for me?
Fishermen, outcasts, farmers, and the like,
whose minds are fixed merely on their own livelihood,
endure the hardships of cold, heat, and the like —
how should I not endure [them] for the welfare of the world?
Having vowed to liberate the world
from afflictions, [extending] to the ends
of the ten directions and the sky,
I myself have not been freed from the afflictions.
Not knowing my own capacity,
I was then speaking like a madman.
Therefore, I shall be one who never turns back
in the destruction of the afflictions — always.
In this I shall be tenacious,
and bound by enmity, I shall wage war —
except against that kind of affliction
which is connected with the destruction of [other] afflictions.
Let my entrails spill out, if they will;
let my head fall off, if it must —
but never shall I bow down
before the enemies that are the afflictions.
An ordinary enemy, even when banished,
may establish himself in another region,
from whence, having gathered strength, he returns.
But the enemy that is the affliction has no such recourse.
Where would it go, this one expelled from the mind?
Where would it stay to strive for my destruction?
It is merely my feeble-mindedness that lacks effort.
The wretched afflictions are conquerable by the vision of wisdom.

children.text: na kleśā viṣayeṣu nendriyagaṇe nāpyantarāle sthitā
children.translated_text: The afflictions do not dwell in the sense-objects, nor in the group of senses, nor in the space between,

children.text: nāto 'nyatra kuhasthitāḥ punarime mathnanti kṛtsnaṃ jagat
children.translated_text: nor elsewhere — where then do they dwell, these that torment the entire world?
This is mere illusion! Therefore, release the fear in your heart, and embrace exertion
for the sake of wisdom. Why do you needlessly torment yourself in the hells?
Having thus resolved, I shall make effort
for the sake of practicing the training as taught.
How can there be freedom from disease
for one whose illness is treatable by medicine, if he departs from the physician's instructions?
In the <s>Bodhicaryāvatāra</s>, the fourth chapter on the training of the <s>Bodhisattva</s>. ||
Chapter 5
One who wishes to guard the training
should carefully guard the mind.
The training cannot be guarded
by one who does not guard the fickle mind.
Untamed, maddened elephants
do not cause as much harm here
as the unleashed elephant of the mind
causes in <s>Avīci</s> and the other [hells].
But if the elephant of the mind
is bound on all sides by the rope of mindfulness,
all fear has vanished,
and all good has arrived.
Tigers, lions, elephants, bears,
serpents, and all enemies,
all the wardens of hell,
<s>ḍākinīs</s> and <s>rākṣasas</s> as well —
all of these become bound
by the binding of the mind alone,
and by the taming of the mind alone,
all of them become tamed.
For all fears
and immeasurable sufferings
arise from the mind alone —
thus spoke the Teacher of Truth.
By whom were the weapons in hell
fashioned with effort?
By whom the floor of heated iron?
And from where did those women arise?
All of that arises from the sinful mind —
so declared the Sage.
Therefore, in the three worlds, there is nothing
more fearsome than the mind.
If the perfection of giving consisted in
making the world free from poverty,
since the world is poor even today,
how did the former [<s>Buddhas</s>] accomplish it?
The perfection of giving is said to be
the thought of giving one's all, with its fruit, to all people.
Therefore it is
the mind itself.
Where can fish and the like be taken
so that I might not kill them?
But when the mind of abstention is attained,
that is considered the perfection of morality.
How many wicked ones could I kill,
[they who are] limitless as the sky?
But when the mind of anger is slain,
all enemies are slain.
Where would there be enough leather
to cover the entire earth?
With just the leather of sandals,
the earth is covered.
Likewise, external things
I cannot hold in check;
I shall hold in check my own mind —
what need have I for the others to be checked?
Even combined with speech and body,
a sluggish mind does not yield that fruit
which a single keen mind alone [yields] —
[the attainment of] <s>Brahma</s>-hood and the like.
All recitations and austerities,
even when practiced for a long time,
are performed in vain by a distracted, sluggish mind —
so declared the Omniscient One.
Those who have not cultivated
this secret essence of all <s>dharma</s> — the mind —
wander in vain through the sky,
seeking to destroy suffering and attain happiness.
Therefore, my mind must be
well-maintained and well-guarded by me.
Apart from the vow of guarding the mind,
what use have I for many vows?
Just as one standing amidst the unruly
carefully guards a wound,
so should one, standing amidst wicked people,
always guard the wound of the mind.
If one, fearing even a little pain from a wound,
carefully guards the wound,
should one not [guard] the wound of the mind,
fearing the blow of the crushing mountains [of hell]?
For one who lives with this conduct,
even among wicked people,
even among crowds of women —
the steadfast ascetic is not broken.
Let my gains perish, if they will;
let honor, body, and life [perish];
let other virtues perish —
but never the mind, ever.
To those who wish to guard the mind,
I make this entreaty with joined palms:
Guard mindfulness and clear comprehension
with all effort!
Just as a person afflicted by illness
is incapable of all activities,
so a mind disturbed by those two [lacks]
is incapable of all activities.
What has been heard, reflected upon, and meditated on
by one whose mind lacks clear comprehension,
does not remain in memory —
like water in a pot with holes.
Many who are learned,
faithful, and devoted to effort,
through the fault of lacking clear comprehension,
become stained by transgressions.
By the thief of lacking clear comprehension,
which follows upon the theft of mindfulness,
even those who have accumulated merits
are robbed and go to bad destinies.
This band of affliction-thieves
searches for an opening.
Having found an opening, they rob
and destroy the life of good destinies.
Therefore, mindfulness should never
be removed from the door of the mind.
If it has departed, it should be restored,
by recollecting the suffering of the lower realms.
For the fortunate ones
who are respectful through reverence and fear,
guided by the teacher's instruction,
mindfulness arises easily through association with the guru.
<s>Buddhas</s> and <s>Bodhisattvas</s>
have unobstructed vision everywhere.
Everything is before them;
I stand in their presence.
Reflecting thus, one should remain
endowed with shame, respect, and fear.
The recollection of the <s>Buddha</s> too
will thus arise for such a person again and again.
Clear comprehension then comes
and, once come, does not depart again,
when mindfulness stands
at the door of the mind for the purpose of guarding.
First, then, this mind should always
be kept in this manner:
I should remain always as if
without senses, like a block of wood.
Fruitless glances of the eyes
should never be made.
The gaze should be kept constantly
directed downward, as if in meditation.
But for the purpose of resting the eyes,
one may occasionally look at the directions.
And upon seeing a mere semblance [of someone],
one should look up in order to greet.
On the road and the like, for the purpose of being aware of danger,
one should repeatedly look in the four directions.
One should look at the directions while resting,
and also look behind by turning around.
Whether going forward or going back,
having examined what is ahead and behind,
thus in all situations,
one should act having understood what is to be done.
Having set the body in position thus,
then again taking up the activity,
'How is the body positioned?' —
this should be checked again in between.
The maddened elephant of the mind
should be examined with all effort,
so that, bound to the great pillar of <s>dharma</s>-contemplation,
it is not released.
'Where is my [mind] abiding?' —
the mind should be thus examined,
so that the yoke of concentration
is not abandoned even for a moment.
In situations of danger or festivity,
if one is unable, one may be at ease.
For at the time of giving,
the relaxation of moral discipline is taught.
Having understood [a task] and begun to undertake it,
one should not think about anything else.
That very thing should be accomplished first,
with the inner self absorbed in it.
In this way, everything will be well done;
otherwise, neither [task] will succeed.
And the affliction of lacking clear comprehension
will also increase in this way.
Amidst the various kinds of idle chatter
occurring in many ways,
and amidst all objects of curiosity,
one should destroy the eagerness that has arisen.
Kneading earth, cutting grass,
drawing lines, and other fruitless [activities] that arise —
remembering the training of the <s>Tathāgata</s>,
one should abandon them at once, out of fear.
Whenever one wishes to move
or even wishes to speak,
one should first examine one's own mind
and act properly with steadfastness.
When one sees one's own mind
to be attached or averse,
one should neither act nor speak;
one should remain like a block of wood.
When [the mind] is haughty, or scornful,
or filled with pride and arrogance,
or given to derision and excess, or crooked,
or deceitful —
when it assumes the appearance of self-aggrandizement
and the disparagement of others,
when it is contentious and aggressive —
one should remain like a block of wood.
When my mind seeks gain, honor, and fame,
or again seeks a retinue,
or seeks attendance —
therefore I shall remain like a block of wood.
When my mind, harsh toward the interests of others,
seeking its own interest,
or wishing to speak for the sake of an audience —
therefore I shall remain like a block of wood.
Impatient, lazy, timid,
impudent, garrulous,
or biased toward one's own faction —
therefore I shall remain like a block of wood.
Thus, seeing the mind to be defiled
or engaged in fruitless endeavors,
the hero should firmly restrain it
always with the antidote.
Firmly resolved, serene,
steadfast, respectful and reverent,
modest, fearful, and peaceful,
devoted to pleasing others —
unwearied by the mutually contradictory
childish desires [of beings],
understanding that these arise from afflictions —
thus [one should be] endowed with compassion.
Always subject to myself and to beings,
in blameless matters,
I shall maintain this mind
like an emanation, free from pride.
Remembering again and again
this excellent moment, obtained after so long,
I shall maintain this mind
immovable, like Mount <s>Sumeru</s>.
When the body is being dragged here and there
by vultures greedy for flesh,
it does not resist —
why then do you come to its defense?
Why do you guard this [body], O mind,
appropriating it and treating it with pride?
If it is indeed separate from you,
then what loss is there to you in this matter?
O fool, you do not claim as your own
a clean wooden puppet;
why do you guard this foul machine
constructed of filth?
First, with your own understanding,
separate this sheath of skin.
With the sword of wisdom,
release the flesh from the cage of bones.
Having separated even the bones,
look at the marrow within.
'Is there any essence here?' —
investigate for yourself.
Having thus searched with effort,
if no essence is found therein by you,
then say: why do you
still guard the body even now?
The impure [flesh] cannot be eaten by you;
the blood cannot be drunk;
the entrails cannot be sucked —
what will you do with the body?
It is fitting to preserve it
as food for vultures, jackals, and the like.
But this body of human beings
is [merely] an instrument for action.
Even as you guard it thus,
merciless death, snatching it away,
will give the body to the vultures —
what then will you do?
To a servant who will not stay,
clothes and the like are not given.
The body will depart after consuming [its provisions] —
why do you incur the expense?
Therefore, having given it its wages,
now attend to your own purpose, O mind!
For not everything earned by a hired worker
is given to him.
Without imposing the notion of a boat upon the body,
from the certainty of going and coming,
make the body go wherever you wish
for the accomplishment of beings' welfare.
One who has thus disciplined the self
should always have a smiling face,
should abandon frowning and knitting of brows,
be the first to speak, and be a friend of the world.
One should not throw down seats and the like
suddenly with a loud noise;
nor should one bang doors —
one should always delight in silence.
The heron, the cat, and the thief,
moving silently and stealthily,
achieve their desired aim —
thus should the practitioner always conduct himself.
From those skilled in exhorting others,
who render help unasked,
one should accept their words with bowed head;
one should always be a pupil to all.
To all well-spoken words
one should utter 'Well said!';
and seeing one who performs meritorious deeds,
one should delight him with praises.
One should speak of [others'] virtues in their absence,
and repeat them with approval;
and when one's own virtue is being praised,
one should reflect on the other's knowledge of virtues.
For all undertakings are for the sake of satisfaction,
which is difficult to obtain even with wealth.
Therefore I shall enjoy the happiness of satisfaction
through the virtues produced by others' efforts.
In this, there is no loss for me,
and in the hereafter, great happiness;
but through hatred [comes] the suffering of displeasure,
and great suffering in the hereafter.
One should speak with words placed confidently and clearly,
with meaning that is distinct and pleasing,
pleasant to the ear, rooted in compassion,
soft and gentle in tone.
One should always look at beings directly,
as if drinking them in with the eyes;
relying on these very [beings],
my <s>Buddhahood</s> will come about.
Great merit arises from constant and earnest [practice],
and from that which arises through its antidote [to afflictions],
and in the field of those with virtues and those who help,
and toward the suffering.
One should be skillful, energetic,
and always act independently;
no room should be given
to anyone in any task.
The <s>pāramitās</s> (perfections), beginning with <s>dāna</s> (giving),
are progressively more excellent;
one should not abandon a higher one for a lesser,
except for the bridge of conduct.
Having understood thus, one should
be constantly engaged in the welfare of others;
even what is prohibited is permitted
for the compassionate one who sees the purpose.
Having shared with those fallen into misfortune, the protectorless,
and with those observing vows,
one should eat a moderate amount;
one should give away everything except the three robes.
One should not torment the body, which serves the true <s>Dharma</s>,
for a trivial purpose;
for in this way alone
one will quickly fulfill the hopes of beings.
Therefore, one should not sacrifice one's life
when the compassionate disposition is impure;
but when the disposition is equal [i.e., mature],
it should be sacrificed — thus there is no loss.
One should not teach the <s>Dharma</s> to one who shows no respect, who is healthy,
nor to one with a cloth-wrapped head,
nor to one carrying an umbrella, staff, or weapon,
nor to one with a veiled head.
The profound and vast [Dharma should not be taught] to the lowly,
nor to women without a man present;
toward lower and higher teachings
one should maintain equal respect.
One should not direct a vessel of the vast <s>Dharma</s>
to a lower teaching;
nor should one, abandoning proper conduct,
entice with <s>sūtras</s> and <s>mantras</s>.
The discarding of a tooth-stick or of spittle
uncovered [i.e., openly]
is not proper — in water, on usable land,
and urinating and the like [openly] is also censured.
One should not eat with the mouth full,
noisily, or with the mouth wide open;
one should not sit with legs dangling,
nor rub both arms simultaneously.
One should not travel, lie down, or sit
alone with another man's wife;
everything that displeases the public —
having observed and inquired, one should avoid.
One should not point with a finger;
rather, respectfully, with the right hand,
with the entire palm,
one should indicate the way and the like.
One should not call someone with vigorous arm-waving
when there is slight urgency;
one should snap the fingers or the like —
otherwise one would be undisciplined.
One should lie down in the desired direction,
as in the Lord's <s>nirvāṇa</s>-posture,
with full awareness, and rise quickly;
beforehand, with determination as a rule.
The conduct of <s>bodhisattvas</s>
is declared to be immeasurable;
but of conduct that purifies the mind,
one should certainly practice that.
Day and night, one should practice the <s>triskandha</s> (threefold confession)
three times;
through that, and relying on the <s>bodhicitta</s> and the <s>Jinas</s>,
the remaining transgressions are pacified.
Whatever situations one encounters,
whether by oneself or under others' control,
whatever trainings apply in those situations —
one should practice those with effort.
For there is nothing whatsoever
that the children of the <s>Jinas</s> should not train in;
there is nothing that is not meritorious
for one who lives thus.
Either directly or indirectly,
one should do nothing except for the welfare of beings;
and for the welfare of beings alone
one should dedicate everything to awakening.
One should never abandon the spiritual friend,
even at the cost of one's life —
one who upholds the <s>bodhisattva</s> vows
and is skilled in the meaning of the <s>Mahāyāna</s>.
From the <s>Śrīsaṃbhava-vimokṣa</s>,
one should learn proper conduct toward the teacher;
this and other teachings of the <s>Buddha</s>
should be known through reading the <s>sūtras</s>.
The trainings are found in the <s>sūtras</s>,
therefore one should read the <s>sūtras</s>;
and in the <s>Ākāśagarbha Sūtra</s>
one should examine the root transgressions.
The <s>Śikṣāsamuccaya</s> (Compendium of Training) must
certainly be examined again and again,
because the right conduct is
shown there in detail.
Or, for the time being, in brief,
one should look at the <s>Sūtrasamuccaya</s>;
and with effort, [examine] the second one
composed by the noble <s>Nāgārjuna</s>.
From what one is restrained, where,
and to what one is enjoined —
having looked at the training,
one should practice it for the protection of worldly minds.
This, in brief, is the defining characteristic
of mindful awareness (<s>saṃprajanya</s>):
the repeated examination
of the state of body and mind.
I shall study with the body [through practice];
for what use is mere verbal recitation?
What will become of the sick
by merely reading the prescription?

children.text: iti bodhicaryāvatāre saṃprajanyarakṣaṇaṃ nāma pañcamaḥ paricchedaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus ends the fifth chapter, called 'The Guarding of Mindful Awareness,' in the <s>Bodhicaryāvatāra</s>. ||
Chapter 6
All this good conduct,
giving, worship of the <s>Sugatas</s>,
performed over thousands of <s>kalpas</s> —
a single moment of hatred destroys it.
There is no evil equal to hatred,
and no austerity equal to patience;
therefore one should cultivate patience
with effort, by various methods.
The mind finds no peace,
nor enjoys pleasure or happiness,
nor finds sleep or steadiness,
when the thorn of hatred dwells in the heart.
Even those whom one honors with wealth and respect,
even those who depend upon him —
even they wish to kill
a master made wretched by hatred.
Even friends are repelled by him;
he gives, yet is not attended upon;
in short, there is nothing
by which an angry person can be well-situated.
Knowing that hatred causes
such sufferings and more,
one who steadfastly destroys anger
is happy in this life and the next.
Finding nourishment in the mental distress
that arises from the occurrence of what is unpleasant
and the obstruction of what is pleasant,
hatred grows strong and destroys me.
Therefore I shall destroy
the nourishment of this enemy;
for this foe has no other task
than to slay me.
Even if the most unpleasant thing should occur,
my cheerfulness should not be disturbed;
for in mental distress there is nothing desirable,
and virtue is undermined.
If there is a remedy,
what is the use of mental distress?
And if there is no remedy,
what is the use of mental distress?
Suffering, contempt, harsh words,
and disrepute — these are unwanted
for oneself or for those one loves;
for one's enemy, it is the reverse.
Happiness is obtained with difficulty;
suffering persists effortlessly;
and only through suffering is there release —
therefore, O mind, be firm!
The devotees of <s>Durgā</s> and the <s>Karṇāṭakas</s>
endure the pain of burning, cutting, and the like
needlessly, for the sake of [supposed] liberation;
why then should I be a coward?
There is nothing
that is difficult for one who practices;
therefore, by practicing with mild discomfort,
even great suffering should be endured.
The pain of gadflies, horseflies, and mosquitoes,
of hunger and thirst and the like,
and great suffering such as itching and the like —
do you not see it as purposeless?
Through cold, heat, rain, wind, sickness,
imprisonment, and beatings,
one should not become delicate —
otherwise, the distress increases.
Some, upon seeing their own blood,
become especially bold;
while others, upon seeing even another's blood,
fall into a faint.
That comes from the firmness
or the timidity of the mind;
therefore one should be a conqueror of suffering
and should overcome pain.
Even in suffering, the wise person
should not disturb the serenity of the mind;
for the battle is with the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions),
and in battle, wounds are easy to come by.
Those who, receiving the enemy's blows on their chests,
conquer their foes —
they alone are the victorious heroes;
the rest are merely slayers of the dead.
There is another virtue of suffering:
through the sense of urgency, pride is dispelled;
compassion arises toward those in <s>saṃsāra</s>,
fear of sin, and longing for the <s>Jina</s>.
I am not angry at bile and the like,
though they cause great suffering;
why then be angry at sentient beings?
They too are provoked by conditions.
Just as this illness arises
even though unwanted,
so too anger arises forcefully
even though unwanted.
Without thinking 'I shall be angry,'
a person becomes angry involuntarily;
and anger does not arise
having first resolved 'I shall arise.'
Whatever offenses there may be
and whatever various sins,
all arise from the force of conditions;
nothing is independent.
The assemblage of conditions does not think
'I shall produce [this]';
nor does the produced [thing] think
'I have been produced.'
That which is called the principal (<s>pradhāna</s>),
and that which is imagined as the self —
even that does not come into being
having thought 'I shall become.'
For what is not yet born does not exist;
who then would wish to come into being?
And since it is occupied with its object,
it does not even strive to cease.
For the self [as they posit it] is eternal, non-conscious,
and clearly inactive, like space;
even in conjunction with other conditions,
what activity can there be for something that is changeless?
If it is the same at the time of action as before,
what has action done to it?
If we say 'its action' is the connection,
which of the two is the basis of that?
Thus everything is dependent on others;
and that on which it depends is itself dependent;
like magical creations — toward things that are
thus inactive, where is there cause for anger?
'If everything is thus [conditioned], then prevention too is not proper —
who prevents what?' — if so objected,
[the answer is:] it is proper, because dependently [arising],
the cessation of suffering is accepted.
Therefore, whether seeing an enemy or a friend
acting wrongly,
one should think 'Such are his conditions' —
reflecting thus, one should be happy.
If all beings could accomplish their goals
merely by their own wish,
then no one would have any suffering,
for no one wishes for suffering.
Through carelessness, people harm themselves
with thorns and the like;
through anger, with breaking food-vessels and the like;
through craving for a hard-to-win woman and the like.
Through hanging, throwing themselves from heights,
through consuming poison and unwholesome food,
some kill themselves,
and through sinful conduct.
When, under the power of afflictions,
they even kill their own dear selves,
how then would they refrain
from [harming] the bodies of others?
Toward those who, maddened by afflictions,
engage in self-destruction —
not only is there no compassion,
but how can anger arise?
If it is the nature of the childish
to cause harm to others,
then anger toward them is not proper for me,
just as toward fire whose nature is to burn.
If, on the other hand, this fault is adventitious
and beings are by nature gentle,
then that anger is equally improper,
as [anger] toward acrid smoke in the sky.
If, setting aside the primary [cause] — the stick and the like —
one is angry at the instigator,
he too is impelled by hatred;
better that my hatred be toward the hatred [itself].
I too have previously
caused just such suffering to beings;
therefore it is fitting for me,
who have caused harm to beings, [to endure this].
Both his weapon and my body
are causes of suffering;
he has taken up the weapon, I have taken up the body —
at which should I be angry?
This body, shaped like a wound,
unable to bear even a touch, I have grasped,
blinded by craving — so in this suffering,
at what should I be angry?
I do not want suffering, yet foolishly
I desire the cause of suffering;
when suffering comes through my own fault,
why be angry at another?
Just as the forest of sword-leaves [in hell]
and the hellish birds
are produced by my own <s>karma</s>,
so too is this [suffering] — at what should I be angry?
Impelled by my own <s>karma</s>,
those who harm me have arisen;
since they will go to hell because of this,
have I not indeed destroyed them?
Relying on these [enemies], my sin
is greatly diminished through patience;
but relying on me, they go
to hells of long suffering.
It is I who harm them,
and they who benefit me;
why then, reversing [the truth],
do you rage, O wicked mind?
If the merit of my intention [protects me]
so that I do not go to hell,
what benefit accrues to them
if I [merely] protect myself?
But if I were to retaliate,
even so, these [senses] are not guarded,
and my practice declines as well;
therefore I am a wretched ascetic, lost.
The mind, being formless,
cannot be killed by anyone anywhere;
but due to its attachment to the body,
it is afflicted by the body's sufferings.
Contempt, harsh words,
and disgrace — this group of [harms]
does not injure the body; therefore,
O mind, why do you become enraged?
The displeasure of others toward me —
will it devour me
in this life or in another,
that I should find it so unwelcome?
If it is unwelcome because it obstructs my gain,
even so,
my gain will perish right here in this life,
but sin will surely remain.
Better that I die right now
than live long by wrong livelihood;
for even after living long,
the suffering of death comes just the same.
One who in a dream enjoys happiness
for a hundred years and then awakens,
and another who enjoys happiness
for a moment and then awakens —
surely for both, upon awakening,
that happiness does not return;
the same comparison applies at the time of death
to the long-lived and the short-lived alike.
Even having obtained many gains
and enjoyed pleasures for a long time,
I shall depart empty-handed and naked,
as if robbed.
If through my gain I live and perform
the destruction of sin and the accumulation of merit,
is it not that getting angry for the sake of gain
brings the destruction of merit and the accumulation of sin?
If that very [purpose] for which I live
is itself destroyed,
what use is that life
which produces nothing but evil?
If hatred toward one who speaks ill of you
[is justified] because he drives beings away, [you say,]
then toward one who brings disgrace upon others,
why does your anger not arise in the same way?
When another's displeasure depends on others,
you are patient with those who are displeased;
but toward one who speaks ill, whose [speech] depends
on the arising of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), you are not patient.
Toward those who revile and destroy images,
<s>stūpas</s>, and the true <s>dharma</s>,
my hatred is not justified,
for the <s>Buddhas</s> and others suffer no harm.
Toward those who harm one's teachers,
relatives, and loved ones,
seeing that [the harm] arises from conditions as before,
one should restrain anger.
Embodied beings inevitably suffer pain
caused by both sentient and insentient [agents];
that pain is [only] perceived in the sentient —
therefore, be patient with this pain.
Some offend out of delusion,
others, equally deluded, become angry;
whom among them shall we call blameless,
and whom shall we call at fault?
Why did you formerly act in such a way
that you are now harmed by others?
All are dependent on <s>karma</s> —
who am I to alter this?
Having understood this, I shall strive
for merit in such a way
that all beings may become
of friendly mind toward one another.
Just as when a house is burning,
fire, having reached an adjacent house,
catches on grass and the like —
those are pulled away and removed;
so too, when the mind is being burned
by the fire of hatred through attachment,
at that very moment it should be abandoned,
for fear of burning the merit-body.
If one condemned to death is set free with only a hand cut off,
is that not fortunate?
If by human sufferings one is freed from the hells,
is that not fortunate?
If even this much suffering
today cannot be endured,
then why is anger, the cause
of hellish torment, not restrained?
For the sake of anger, just so,
I have been cast into the hells thousands of times,
and have accomplished neither my own purpose
nor the purpose of others.
This suffering is not of that [terrible] kind,
and it will accomplish a great purpose;
in suffering that removes the suffering of the world,
only joy is appropriate.
If others have obtained the pleasure of joy
by praising one rich in virtues,
O mind, you too, by praising him —
why do you not likewise rejoice?
And this joy-pleasure of yours
is blameless, a source of happiness,
not prohibited by the virtuous,
and the supreme means of winning others over.
If [you think] 'It is only his happiness' —
if this is not pleasing to you,
then by ceasing to pay wages and the like,
both seen and unseen [results] would be destroyed.
When your own virtues are praised,
you wish for the pleasure of others;
when the virtues of others are praised,
you do not wish even for your own pleasure.
Having generated <s>bodhicitta</s>
with the wish for the happiness of all beings,
why do you now become angry
at beings who have obtained happiness on their own?
Do you not wish <s>Buddhahood</s> for beings,
which is worshipped by the three worlds?
Seeing them receive some small honor,
why do you burn?
He who nourishes one whom you should nourish
is giving to you indeed;
having found one who supports your household,
you are not pleased but angry!
What does he not wish for beings,
who wishes them <s>bodhi</s> (awakening)?
How can he have <s>bodhicitta</s>
who becomes angry at another's good fortune?
If [the gift] was not received by him,
it remains in the donor's house;
in any case it is not yours —
what does it matter to you whether given or not?
Should he obstruct his merits,
or those well-disposed toward his virtues,
or should he not accept what he is receiving?
Tell me — with whom are you not angry?
Not only do you not grieve for yourself,
a sinner,
but you wish to compete
with others who have performed merit!
Even if something unpleasant befalls your enemy,
what reason is there for your satisfaction?
Your mere wish alone
will not become a cause [of his harm].
And even if it were accomplished by your wish,
what happiness is there for you in his suffering?
Even if there were some benefit in this,
what greater harm could there be than this?
For this is the dreadful hook
cast by the fisherman of the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions),
from which the guardians of hell,
having bought you, will cook you in cauldrons.
Praise, fame, and honor
serve me neither for merit nor for long life,
neither for strength nor for health,
nor for bodily comfort.
These would be the extent of one's own welfare
for a wise person who knows his own good;
if one desires mental pleasure,
one might as well resort to liquor and gambling.
For the sake of fame, some squander wealth
and even kill themselves;
can syllables [of praise] be eaten?
Once dead, whose is that pleasure?
Just as a child wails bitterly
when his sand-castle collapses,
so my mind appears to me
at the loss of praise and fame.
Since a sound has no consciousness,
it is impossible that 'it praises me';
but [you say,] 'another is pleased with me' —
this is the cause of my pleasure.
Whether the pleasure is in another or in me,
what benefit is another's pleasure to me?
That pleasure of joy belongs to him alone;
not even the slightest share of it is mine.
If I am happy because of his happiness,
then let that [attitude] apply in all cases;
why am I not happy when others are made happy
by the favor of someone else?
Therefore, the pleasure that arises in oneself
[thinking] 'I am being praised' —
since there too there is no real connection,
is merely childish behavior.
Praise and the like destroy my composure
and my sense of spiritual urgency;
they produce jealousy toward the virtuous
and anger at their success.
Therefore, those who stand ready
to destroy praise and the like directed at me —
are they not engaged
in protecting me from falling into lower realms?
For one seeking liberation, the bondage
of gain and honor is unfitting for me;
those who free me from bondage —
how can I hate them?
Those who have become like a door barring me
as I wish to enter suffering —
as if stationed by the <s>Buddhas</s> themselves —
how can I hate them?
'He has created an obstacle to my merit' —
anger here is not justified;
there is no austerity equal to patience —
is this not the very occasion for it?
If through my own fault
I fail to practice patience here,
then it is I who have created the obstacle,
when the cause of merit was at hand.
That which does not exist without [something],
and which exists when [that thing] is present —
that very [thing] is its cause;
how can it be called an obstacle?
For a beggar appearing at the right time
is no obstacle to giving;
nor when one meets a renunciant
is it called an obstacle to renunciation.
Beggars are easily found in the world,
but those who do harm are rare;
for if I have done no wrong,
no one will wrong me.
Therefore, like a treasure arisen in the house
without effort,
my enemy is to be cherished
as a companion on the path to awakening.
This fruit of patience has been produced
by me and by him together;
therefore, to him it should first be given,
since patience originates with him.
If the enemy is not to be honored because
he has no intention of [helping me achieve] patience,
then how is the true <s>dharma</s> honored,
which is [also] a mere fit cause of [spiritual] accomplishment?
If the enemy is not to be honored because
his intention is to cause harm,
how else would patience arise in me —
as toward a doctor intent on healing?
Since patience arises
dependent on his hostile intention,
he is indeed the cause of patience
and should be honored by me like the true <s>dharma</s>.
The field of beings is the field of the <s>Jinas</s> (Conquerors) —
thus has the Sage declared,
for by gratifying these [beings], many
have gone to the far shore of perfection.
Since attaining the qualities of the <s>Buddhas</s>
is equally [dependent] on beings and on the <s>Jinas</s>,
what justification is there for honoring the <s>Jinas</s>
but not beings?
The greatness of [the <s>Jinas</s>'] intention
lies not in itself but in its effect;
and [beings'] greatness is equal in that respect —
therefore beings are equal [to the <s>Jinas</s>].
That one with a friendly intention is to be honored —
that is the very greatness of beings;
that merit comes from faith in the <s>Buddhas</s> —
that is the very greatness of the <s>Buddhas</s>.
By their share in [enabling] the attainment of the <s>Buddha</s>-qualities,
therefore beings are equal to the <s>Jinas</s>;
yet none are truly equal to the <s>Buddhas</s>,
who are oceans of infinite aspects of virtue.
If even a tiny quality is seen anywhere
in those who are the sole treasures of the essence of virtues,
to honor that [quality],
even the three worlds would not suffice.
But the best share — [the capacity for] the arising of <s>Buddha</s>-qualities —
exists in beings;
in proportion to this share,
let the worship of beings be performed.
Moreover, toward those genuine friends
of immeasurable beneficence,
what higher repayment could there be
than gratifying beings?
For those for whose sake they break their bodies
