children.translated_text: and enter <s>Avīci</s> — when done for them, it is done;
therefore, toward these [beings], even those who do great harm,
one should practice only what is beneficial.
My masters themselves, after all,
are indifferent even to their own selves for those [beings'] sake;
how then can I display pride
toward those very masters, rather than the attitude of a servant?
The chief sages rejoice in their happiness
and are pained at their suffering;
by pleasing them, all the chief sages are pleased;
by harming them, the sages are offended.
Just as one whose body is ablaze on all sides
finds no delight even in all pleasures,
so too, when beings suffer,
there is no means of pleasing the compassionate ones.
Therefore, whatever sin I have committed
against all the great compassionate ones by causing suffering to beings,
that sin I now confess;
may the sages whom I have distressed forgive me.
For the sake of pleasing the <s>Tathāgatas</s>,
today I enter into servitude to the world with my whole being;
let the throngs of people place their feet on my head
or strike me — may the Lord of the World be pleased.
There is no doubt that the compassionate ones
have made this entire world their own;
those seen in the form of beings
are the protectors themselves — why disrespect them?
This alone is the worship of the <s>Tathāgatas</s>;
this alone is the accomplishment of one's own purpose;
this alone is the removal of the world's suffering —
therefore, let this alone be my vow.
Just as a single king's officer
oppresses a great multitude,
the far-sighted multitude
is unable to retaliate;
for he is not alone —
the king's power is his power.
So too, one should not disregard
any weak person who has offended;
for the guardians of hell
and the compassionate ones are his power.
Therefore, one should gratify beings
as a servant [gratifies] a wrathful king.
What could an angry king do
that would equal the suffering of hell
which is experienced as a result
of causing displeasure to beings?
What could a pleased king give
that would equal <s>Buddhahood</s>,
which is experienced as a result
of causing delight to beings?
Setting aside the future <s>Buddhahood</s>
that arises from gratifying beings,
do you not see the good fortune, fame,
and well-being [that come] even in this life?
Beauty, health,
joy, and long life,
and the abundant happiness of a universal monarch —
the patient one obtains while wandering in <s>saṃsāra</s>.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Perfection of Patience (<s>Kṣāntipāramitā</s>), in the <s>Bodhicaryāvatāra</s>. ||
Chapter 7
Thus patient, one should take up vigor,
for awakening (<s>bodhi</s>) abides in vigor;
without vigor there is no merit,
just as without wind there is no movement.
What is vigor? Enthusiasm for the wholesome.
What is said to be its opposite?
Laziness, attachment to the base,
despondency, and self-contempt.
Through the craving for the pleasure of idleness,
the taste for inactivity, and reliance on sleep,
through lack of distress at the sufferings of <s>saṃsāra</s>,
laziness arises.
Sniffed by the trap of the afflictions,
you have entered the snare of birth.
Do you still not realize
that you have come into the jaws of death?
Do you not see those of your own kind
being killed one by one?
And yet you go right on sleeping,
like a buffalo before a butcher.
When <s>Yama</s> is watching you
and all your paths are blocked,
how can you take pleasure in eating?
How can you sleep? How can you delight?
As soon as you have gathered your provisions,
death will come swiftly.
Even if you abandon your laziness then,
what will you do when it is too late?
'This has not been achieved; that has been begun;
this stands half-done' —
death has come suddenly!
Thinking 'Alas, I am ruined!' —
seeing your relatives with faces swollen from
the rush of grief, eyes red with tears,
seeing them despairing,
and the faces of <s>Yama</s>'s messengers —
tormented by the memory of your own sins,
hearing the cries of hell,
your body smeared with excrement from terror —
in your distress, what will you do?
'I am like a living fish' —
your fear in this very life is justified.
How much more so for one who has sinned,
from the intense sufferings of hell?
O tender one, you are scalded
even when touched by hot water.
Having performed actions that lead to hell,
how can you sit at ease like this?
O tender one who desires fruit without effort,
of much suffering,
seized by death yet putting on the appearance of an immortal —
alas, suffering one, you are being destroyed!
Having found the boat of a human birth,
cross the great river of suffering!
O fool, this is no time for sleep —
this boat is hard to find again.
Having abandoned the supreme delight of the <s>Dharma</s>,
an unending stream of joy,
how can you take delight in frivolity and laughter,
which are causes of suffering?
Non-dejection, the array of powers, earnestness, self-mastery,
equality of self and other,
and the exchange of self and other —
One should not lose heart, thinking
'How can awakening be for me?'
For the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the speaker of truth,
spoke this truth:
Even those who were gadflies, mosquitoes,
bees, and worms
attained, through the force of effort,
the supreme, hard-to-attain awakening.
How much more so I, born a human being,
capable of knowing what is beneficial and what is harmful —
without abandoning the practice of the Omniscient One,
why should I not attain awakening?
Even if there is the fear that
'I must give my hands, feet, and the like' —
that is confusion about what is weighty and what is light,
arising from lack of discernment.
I shall be cut, broken,
burned, and split open, many times over,
for countless millions of aeons —
and there will be no awakening [without that].
But this limited suffering of mine
is the means to complete awakening —
like the pain of extracting
a splinter in order to remove a deeper agony.
All physicians bring about health
through treatments that cause pain.
Therefore, to destroy great sufferings,
a small [suffering] must be endured.
But the supreme physician has not prescribed
even this usual treatment.
He treats the gravely ill
with the gentlest of methods.
At first, the Guide enjoins
the giving of vegetables and the like.
Gradually one progresses until
one can give away even one's own flesh.
When wisdom regarding one's own flesh
arises as [naturally] as regarding vegetables,
then for one who gives up flesh and bone,
what is difficult?
One is not unhappy, having abandoned sin;
one is not dejected, being wise.
For suffering of the mind comes from false imagining,
and suffering of the body from sin.
Through merit the body is happy;
through wisdom the mind is happy.
The compassionate one who remains in <s>saṃsāra</s>
for the sake of others — by what would he be distressed?
Consuming prior sins
and gathering oceans of merit,
by the power of <s>bodhicitta</s> alone
he advances even faster than the <s>Śrāvakas</s>.
Thus going from happiness to happiness,
who with a mind would be dejected?
Having attained the chariot of <s>bodhicitta</s>,
which removes all weariness and fatigue,
the forces of aspiration, steadfastness, delight, and release
are for the accomplishment of the welfare of beings.
One should cultivate aspiration out of fear of suffering
and by contemplating its benefits.
Thus, having uprooted the opposition,
one should strive for the increase of effort
through the forces of aspiration, pride, delight,
release, earnestness, and self-mastery.
Immeasurable are the faults
I must destroy — those of self and others —
and for each single fault,
oceans of aeons [are needed] for its destruction.
Yet in this endeavor to destroy faults,
not even a fraction [of effort] is seen in me.
When I am the vessel for immeasurable suffering,
how does my heart not burst?
Many virtues must be acquired by me
for the sake of self and others.
The practice of each and every virtue
might not be accomplished even in oceans of aeons.
Yet in even a fraction of virtue,
no practice has ever been started by me.
This amazingly obtained birth
has been squandered by me in vain.
I have not attained the joy
of the great festivals of worshipping the Lord.
I have not served the Teaching,
nor fulfilled the wishes of the destitute.
I have not given fearlessness to the frightened,
nor made the afflicted happy.
I have become merely a spike of pain
in my mother's womb, only for suffering.
Through my separation from the desire for <s>Dharma</s>
in previous [lives], this present
calamity has arisen.
Who would abandon the desire for <s>Dharma</s>?
The Sage declared that aspiration is the root
of all wholesome [qualities].
And the root of that, in turn, is the constant
contemplation of the fruits of ripening.
Sufferings, dejections,
and various fears,
and the frustration of desires
arise for those who do evil.
Wherever the wish of doers of good
turns,
there, by their merits,
they are honored with precious fruits.
But wherever the evil-doer's desire for happiness
turns,
there, by his sins,
he is struck by the weapons of suffering.
Dwelling in the heart of a vast, fragrant, cool lotus,
nourished in splendor by the sweet voice of the <s>Jinas</s>,
with noble bodies emerging from the lotus opened by the hands of the Sage —
the sons of the <s>Sugatas</s> come forth before the <s>Sugata</s>, through their merit.
Seized by the minions of <s>Yama</s>, all complexion lost, crying in anguish,
body drenched in molten copper, scorched by the heat of fire,
flesh sliced to pieces by hundreds of blows from blazing swords and spears —
one falls many times upon the red-hot iron ground, through evil deeds.
Therefore, aspiration toward virtue should be cultivated
with devotion, having contemplated thus.
Following the method of [the sūtra of] <s>Vajradhvaja</s>,
one should then cultivate pride.
Having first examined one's resources,
one should undertake [a task] or not.
It is better not to begin at all
than to begin and then turn back.
In future lives too, that habit [of withdrawal] continues,
and suffering from sin increases.
Another opportunity, and the time for action,
will be lost, and the goal will not be accomplished.
Pride should be applied in three areas:
action, afflictions, and capacity.
'By me alone must this be done' —
this is the pride regarding action.
This world, controlled by the afflictions,
is incapable of accomplishing its own welfare.
Therefore I must act on their behalf —
I am not incapable like ordinary people.
When another does a lowly task,
how can I just stand by?
If I do not do it out of pride,
better that my pride should perish.
Finding a dead lizard,
even a crow acts like a <s>Garuḍa</s>.
Even a small misfortune overwhelms me
if my mind is weak.
One who, through dejection, has ceased to act —
is not adversity easy [for such a one]?
But one who has risen up and is striving
is invincible even by great [adversities].
Therefore, with firm resolve,
I shall bring adversity upon adversity.
To wish to conquer the three worlds
while being conquered — that is laughable for me.
I must conquer all,
and I am to be conquered by none.
This pride I must bear —
for I am a son of the lion-like <s>Jinas</s>.
Those beings conquered by pride
are wretched — they are not the truly proud.
The truly proud one does not submit to the enemy [i.e., pride-as-affliction],
but those others are under the sway of the enemy 'pride.'
Led by [that false] pride to lower realms,
even in human existence they are devoid of joy —
slaves eating others' scraps,
fools, ugly, and emaciated.
Scorned by everyone,
those wretched ones, stiffened by [false] pride —
if even they are counted among the proud,
tell me, what kind of wretches are they?

children.text: te mānino vijayinaśca ta eva śūrā
children.translated_text: Those are the truly proud, those are the victors, those the heroes,
who bear pride for the sake of conquering the enemy 'pride' —
who, having slain that swelling enemy 'pride,'
freely bestow the fruit of victory upon the world.
Standing in the midst of the affliction-host,
one should be defiant a thousandfold,
unconquerable by the hosts of afflictions —
like a lion among herds of deer.
Even in great difficulties,
the eye does not perceive [the danger to itself from] flavor.
Likewise, even when encountering difficulty,
one should not come under the power of the afflictions.
Whatever task one undertakes,
one should become absorbed in that task,
intoxicated with it, insatiable —
like one who seeks the pleasure of a game's reward.
Action is performed for the sake of happiness,
yet happiness may or may not result.
But for one whose happiness is action itself,
how can he be happy without action?
There is no satisfaction from desires in <s>saṃsāra</s> —
they are like honey on a razor's edge.
How could there be satiety from the nectar of merit,
sweet in its ripening, auspicious?
Therefore, even when a task is completed,
one should plunge into the next task,
just as an elephant scorched by the midday sun
rushes into a lake the moment it finds one.
But when one's strength is about to fail,
one should set aside [the task] to do again [later].
And when it is well completed, one should leave it,
with the thirst for what comes next.
One should guard against the blows of the afflictions
and strike the afflictions hard —
as if engaged in a sword-fight
with a trained enemy.
Just as in such a fight, one who drops
the sword would quickly pick it up in fear,
so should one pick up the dropped sword of mindfulness,
remembering the hells.
Just as poison that reaches the blood
spreads throughout the body,
so a fault, finding an opening,
spreads throughout the mind.
Just as one carrying a vessel of oil
while surrounded by swordsmen,
from fear of death if one should stumble,
is intent [on not spilling] — so should the practitioner be.
Therefore, just as one quickly rises
when a snake slithers onto one's lap,
so should one quickly counteract
the onset of sleep and laziness.
At each and every lapse,
one should reproach oneself thoroughly and reflect:
'What shall I do so that
this will not happen to me again?'
For this reason, one should seek
association or activity [that supports mindfulness],
[thinking:] 'How can the practice of mindfulness
be maintained in these circumstances?'
One should make oneself light [and ready],
remembering the discourse on heedfulness,
so that before the arrival of action,
one is prepared and present everywhere.
Just as cotton is subject to the coming and going
of the wind,
so should one follow the power of enthusiasm —
and thus does spiritual power (<s>ṛddhi</s>) flourish.
[End of] the seventh chapter, called 'The Perfection of Heroic Effort (<s>Vīryapāramitā</s>),' in the <s>Bodhicaryāvatāra</s>. ||
Chapter 8
Having thus increased one's enthusiasm,
one should stabilize the mind in meditation (<s>samādhi</s>).
For a person with a distracted mind
dwells between the fangs of the afflictions.
Through the seclusion of body and mind,
distraction does not arise.
Therefore, one should abandon the worldly
and set aside discursive thoughts.
The world is not abandoned because of attachment
and craving for gain and the like.
Therefore, in order to abandon these,
the wise person should reflect thus:
Knowing that <s>śamatha</s> (calm abiding) endowed with <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight)
destroys the afflictions,
<s>śamatha</s> should first be sought.
And it [comes] from delight in detachment from the world.
What attachment is fitting
for an impermanent being toward impermanent [beings]?
For thousands of lives, one will not see
the loved one again.
Not seeing [the beloved], one becomes unhappy
and cannot settle in meditation.
Nor is one satisfied even upon seeing —
one is tormented by craving as before.
One does not see [things] as they really are;
one falls away from spiritual urgency.
One is consumed by the grief
of longing for the meeting with the beloved.
By thinking of that, one's short life
passes away in vain, again and again.
Through an impermanent friend,
the eternal <s>Dharma</s> is lost.
One who keeps the company of fools
assuredly goes to a lower realm.
One is led to what is disagreeable —
what is gained from the company of fools?
In an instant they become friends;
in an instant they become enemies.
They grow angry even at what should please them —
ordinary people are hard to gratify.
When told what is beneficial, they grow angry
and turn me away from what is beneficial.
And if they are not heeded,
they go to a lower realm out of anger.
Envy toward the superior, rivalry toward the equal,
arrogance toward the inferior, intoxication from praise,
anger from criticism —
when is there benefit from a fool?
Self-aggrandizement, disparagement of others,
talk about the pleasures of <s>saṃsāra</s> —
some unwholesome thing inevitably
arises from a fool to a fool.
Thus, from the association of one [fool] with another,
there comes a meeting with harm.
I shall dwell alone,
happily, with an unafflicted mind.
One should flee far from fools.
When encountered, one should please them with kindness,
not through the bonds of intimacy,
but like an impartial good person.
Taking only what serves the <s>Dharma</s> —
like a bee [taking] honey from flowers —
I shall dwell everywhere as a stranger,
without intimate connection.
'I am a gainer and honored,
and many desire me' —
for a mortal, such [thoughts]
give rise to fear at death.
Wherever the mind, deluded by pleasure,
takes delight,
that very thing, multiplied a thousandfold,
arises as suffering.
Therefore the wise one should not desire it;
from desire, fear arises.
It passes away of its own accord —
having steadied oneself, let one await it.
Many have been gainers,
and many have been famous.
But together with their gains and fame —
it is not known where they have gone.
Others despise me —
so why should I be pleased when praised?
Others praise me —
so why should I be downcast when blamed?
Beings have diverse dispositions;
even the Conquerors (<s>Jinas</s>) could not please them all.
How much less so an ignorant person like me?
Therefore, what use is concern for the worldly?
They blame one without gains
and disparage one with gains.
With those who are by nature painful to live with,
how can there be delight?
A fool is no one's friend —
so it was said by the <s>Tathāgatas</s> —
because the fool's affection
arises only from self-interest.
Affection that arises through self-interest
is really just love of oneself.
Just as the distress at the loss of property
is caused by the loss of one's own pleasure.
Trees do not disparage
and need not be propitiated with effort.
When shall I dwell together
with those pleasant companions?
Dwelling in empty temples,
at the foot of trees, or in caves —
when shall I depart, without attachment,
never looking back?
In places not claimed by anyone,
naturally vast and open —
dwelling where I please, roaming freely —
when shall I live thus?
Possessing only an earthen bowl,
wearing a robe not worth stealing,
fearless, I shall live —
when? — not concealing this body.
Going to the charnel ground, my body's destined place,
and comparing my own body
with other skeletons —
when [shall I see] it as subject to decay?
For this very body of mine
will become so putrid
that even jackals will not approach it
because of its stench.
Even the bone-fragments
that are born together with this single body
will each scatter apart —
how much more so other dear persons?
One is born alone
and one dies alone.
No one else shares in one's suffering —
what use are friends who create obstacles?
Just as a traveler on the road
takes up a place to stay,
so one traveling the road of existence
takes up a birth as a dwelling.
Before one is carried away from there
by four men,
while the world still mourns —
let one go to the forest at that very time.
Without attachments and without conflicts,
alone in body,
already dead to the world beforehand,
one does not grieve when dying.
And no one nearby stands grieving
and causing distress.
And no one distracts one
from the recollection of the <s>Buddha</s> and the like.
Therefore, delightful solitude,
effortless, the source of all good,
which pacifies all distractions —
should always be cultivated by me.
Freed from all other concerns,
with mind one-pointedly focused on my own mind,
I shall strive for the composure of the mind
and for its taming.
For desires produce harm
in this world and the next:
here, by bondage, beating, and mutilation;
in the next world, in hell and the like.
For the sake of which, with joined palms,
one entreated go-betweens many times,
and for which neither sin
nor ill-repute was counted before.
One cast oneself into danger,
and squandered one's wealth.
And those very ones whom, having embraced,
one found the greatest bliss —
they are nothing but bones, nothing else,
autonomous, belonging to no one.
Embracing them to your heart's content —
why do you not go to bliss [in death]?
That face which was lifted up with effort
and lowered with modesty,
whether seen before or not,
covered with a veil —
that face — as if the vultures, unable to bear
the trouble [of uncovering it],
have now laid it bare — behold!
Why do you flee now?
That which was guarded even from
the falling glances of others —
that is now being devoured —
O jealous one, why do you not protect it?
Seeing this heap of flesh
being devoured by vultures and others,
you worship others' food
with garlands, sandalwood, and ornaments?
You tremble at a motionless skeleton
just seen in this state —
will you not fear one moved about
as if by some <s>vetāla</s> (zombie)?
From the same food [eaten],
both saliva and filth are produced.
If filth is unpleasant to you,
how is drinking saliva pleasant?
Those deluded by desire for impurity
do not delight in pillows
soft to the touch and stuffed with cotton,
because 'they do not exude a foul smell.'
If there is this lust even when [the body is] covered,
why is the uncovered [body] not [equally] pleasant?
If you have no use for the uncovered,
why do you caress what is covered?
If you have no desire for what is impure,
why do you embrace another [body],
a cage of bones bound with sinews,
plastered with the mud of flesh?
You yourself have plenty of impurity —
satisfy yourself with that alone.
O glutton for excrement, forget
that other bag of filth!
'I love the flesh!' you say,
and wish to see and touch it.
But flesh is by nature unconscious —
how can you desire it?
That which you desire — the mind —
cannot be seen or touched.
And that which can [be seen and touched] has no awareness —
why do you embrace it in vain?
That you do not realize another's body
to be made of filth — that is not surprising.
But that you do not realize your own [body]
to be made of filth — that is astonishing!
Leaving aside the young lotus,
opened by the rays of the cloudless sun —
for a mind fond of filth,
what delight is there in a cage of excrement?
If you do not wish to touch
earth and the like smeared with filth,
how can you wish to touch the body
from which that [filth] has issued?
If you have no desire for what is impure,
why do you embrace another [body],
born in a field of filth,
its seed, and nourished by it?
You do not desire a small impure worm
born from filth.
Yet you desire a body made of much filth,
also born from filth?
Not only do you not feel disgust
at your own impurity,
but, O glutton for excrement, you desire
other vessels of filth as well!
Even pleasant things like camphor and the like,
or rice and curries,
when spat out from the mouth,
render even the ground impure.
If you are not convinced
even by this obvious impurity,
look at the other terrible bodies
cast in the charnel ground as well.
Since great fear arises
when the skin is torn open —
how, even knowing this, can desire
arise again for the very same thing?
The fragrance applied to the body
comes from sandalwood alone, not from anything else.
Why is one attracted to something else
by a fragrance belonging to something else?
If, because of its natural foul smell,
there is no attachment — is that not beneficial?
Why does the world, delighting in the harmful,
anoint it with fragrance?
If it is sandalwood that is fragrant,
what has the body contributed here?
Why is one attracted to something else
by a fragrance belonging to something else?
If the body, with long hair and nails,
stained, yellowish teeth,
naked, smeared in the mud of filth,
is naturally terrifying —
why is it adorned with effort,
like a weapon for self-destruction?
The earth is crowded with madmen
busied in deluding themselves.
Having felt revulsion at seeing a few skeletons
in the charnel ground,
you delight in the village-charnel-ground,
teeming with walking skeletons?
And thus this impurity
is not obtained without a price.
For its sake, the toil of earning;
and in hell and the like, suffering.
A child has no power to earn;
by what is one happy in youth?
Youth passes in earning;
what can an old person do with desires?
Some wretched sensualists,
exhausted by a full day's work,
come home in the evening
and lie down like the dead.
Others, afflicted by the suffering
of military campaigns and exile,
do not see their wives and children
even for years, those who desire them.
That for the sake of which
they sold themselves, deluded by desire —
that was not obtained; life was spent in vain
in the service of others.
For those who have sold themselves
and are always doing others' bidding —
their wives give birth [to children of other men]
in forest thickets and the like.
They enter battle, where life is at stake,
indeed, for the sake of a livelihood.
For the sake of honor they go into servitude —
the fools, mocked by desire!
Some sensualists are cut [to pieces],
others are impaled on stakes.
They are seen being burned
and being killed with weapons.
Know wealth to be endless misfortune,
through the grief of gaining, guarding, and losing.
For those whose minds are attached to wealth,
through [their] distraction, there is no opportunity for liberation from the suffering of existence.
Thus the disadvantages of the sensual are many,
and the pleasure is slight —
like the mouthful of grass
seized by the beast drawing the cart.
For the sake of that morsel of pleasure
that is not hard to get even for a beast —
this rare, fortunate moment,
so hard to obtain, has been destroyed by [ill] fate.
For this petty [body] that is sure to perish,
that falls into hell and the like —
all this toil endured
for the sake of the body, through all time.
With even a fraction of that effort,
multiplied a hundred <s>koṭi</s> times, <s>Buddha</s>-hood [could be attained].
The suffering of [worldly] conduct is greater than [the suffering of spiritual] conduct,
and awakening is not [attained] by the sensual.
Neither weapons, nor poison, nor fire,
nor precipices, nor enemies
can compare with desires,
when one recalls the sufferings of hell and the like.
Thus, having become averse to desires,
one should generate delight in solitude —
in the peaceful forest realms,
free from quarrel and toil.
The fortunate ones, on vast stone terraces
of delightful palaces, cooled by moonbeams and sandalwood,
fanned by the silent, gentle forest breeze,
walk about, contemplating the welfare of others.
Dwelling as long as one wishes in empty abodes,
at the foot of trees, in caves —
freed from the weariness of guarding possessions,
one wanders without attachment, as one pleases.
Dwelling where one pleases, roaming freely,
bound to no one —
the contentment and happiness one enjoys
is hard to obtain even for <s>Indra</s>.
Thus, through contemplating the virtues of solitude
in such and other ways,
with discursive thought pacified,
one should cultivate <s>Bodhicitta</s>.
First one should diligently meditate
on the equality of self and other thus:
'All are equal in suffering and happiness;
I should protect them as I do myself.'
Just as the body, though manifold
with its parts such as hands and the like, is to be protected as one,
so too this differentiated world,
undifferentiated in suffering and happiness, is entirely so.
Although my suffering
does not afflict other bodies,
nevertheless that suffering is mine,
unbearable due to self-cherishing.
Likewise, although another's suffering
is not felt by me myself,
nevertheless that suffering is his,
unbearable [to him] due to self-cherishing.
Another's suffering should be dispelled by me
because it is suffering, like my own.
Others should be shown kindness by me
because they are beings, like myself.
When happiness is equally dear
to me and to others,
what is special about the self
that I strive for happiness for it alone?
When fear and suffering are equally disliked
by me and by others,
what is special about the self
that I protect it and not the other?
'Their suffering does not harm me' —
if therefore it is not to be averted,
then the sufferings of my future body too
do not harm me — so why avert them?
'But I shall be the same person then' —
this is a false construction,
since it is one who dies
and quite another who is born.
If it is held that only the one whose suffering it is
should avert it —
the suffering of the foot is not the hand's:
why then is it averted by the hand?
Even if this is unjustified
and proceeds from the sense of 'I' —
what is unjustified should be rejected,
whether regarding self or other, as far as possible.
The continuum and the aggregate
are fictions, like a row or an army.
There is no one to whom suffering belongs —
so whose [suffering] will that be?
All sufferings without exception
are ownerless, without distinction.
They are to be averted because they are suffering.
What use is a fixed rule there?
'Why should suffering be averted?' —
if [asked], all agree, without dispute.
If it is to be averted, then all [suffering] equally so;
if not, then for oneself too, just as for all.
'But compassion produces much suffering' —
if so, why generate it forcibly?
Having reflected on the suffering of the world,
how can the suffering of compassion be great [in comparison]?
If the suffering of one
removes the suffering of many,
then that suffering should be produced
by a compassionate one, for oneself and for others.
Therefore <s>Supuṣpacandra</s>,
even knowing the danger from the king,
did not destroy his own suffering
at the expense of those many who suffered.
Those whose continua are thus cultivated,
holding the suffering of others as equally dear,
they plunge into <s>Avīci</s>
as swans [plunge] into a lotus pond.
When beings are being liberated,
those oceans of joy [that arise] —
are they not alone sufficient?
What need is there for flavorless liberation?
Therefore, even having acted for the sake of others,
there is no pride and no wonder,
no expectation of the fruit of ripening —
through the sole thirst for the welfare of others.
Therefore, just as I protect myself
from even the slightest blame,
so too toward others I shall cultivate
a mind of protection and a mind of compassion.
Through habituation, in another's
drops of semen and blood,
there arises the notion 'I am' —
even though the thing [so identified] does not [truly] exist.
Likewise, why should another's body
not be apprehended as 'self'?
The otherness of one's own body
is well established and not difficult [to grasp].
Having recognized oneself as full of faults
and others as oceans of virtues,
one should meditate on the abandonment of self-identity
and the adoption of others [as oneself].
Just as the hands and the like are cherished
as members of the body,
why are embodied beings not [cherished] likewise
as members of the world?
Just as the notion of self arises through habituation
in this selfless body of one's own,
why should selfhood not arise in others too
through habituation?
Thus, even having acted for the sake of others,
there is no pride and no wonder.
Just as when one has fed oneself,
no expectation of a reward arises.
Therefore, just as you wish to protect yourself
from affliction, grief, and the like,
so too let a mind of protection and a mind of compassion
be cultivated toward the world.
For this reason the Protector
named <s>Avalokita</s> consecrated even his own name
to remove the fear of timidity
of people even in assemblies.
One should not turn back from what is difficult,
for through the power of habituation,
that whose very name once caused terror
becomes that without which there is no delight.
One who wishes to quickly rescue
both oneself and others
should practice the supreme secret:
the exchange of self and other.
Because of excessive attachment to this self,
fear arises even from the slightest danger.
Who would not hate this self
which, like an enemy, brings fear?
He who, wishing to remedy
hunger, thirst, and the like of the body,
kills birds, fish, and deer,
and lies in ambush [on the road] —
he who, for the sake of gain and honor,
would kill even his own parents,
and steal the property of the Three Jewels,
whereby he would become fuel for <s>Avīci</s> —
what wise person would desire, protect,
or worship such a self?
Who would not see it as an enemy?
And who would honor it?
'If I give, what shall I eat?' —
this selfishness is the way of demons.
'If I eat, what shall I give?' —
this concern for others is the way of the king of gods.
Having harmed another for one's own sake,
one is cooked in the hells and the like.
But having afflicted oneself for the sake of others,
one attains all prosperity.
Bad destiny, low birth, and stupidity [come]
from the very desire to elevate oneself.
Transferring that [desire] to others,
[one attains] good destiny, honor, and wisdom.
By commanding another for one's own sake,
one experiences servitude and the like.
But by commanding oneself for the sake of others,
one experiences mastery and the like.
All who are miserable in the world
are so from seeking their own happiness.
All who are happy in the world
are so from seeking the happiness of others.
But what need is there to say more?
Just see this difference:
between the fool who seeks his own interest
and the sage who acts for the interest of others.
Not to speak of attaining <s>Buddhahood</s> —
even happiness in <s>saṃsāra</s> is impossible
for one who does not exchange
one's own happiness for the suffering of others.
Let alone the next world —
even one's visible aim is not accomplished
when a servant does not work
and the master does not pay wages.
Having abandoned the mutual production of happiness
— the festival of happiness both seen and unseen —
the deluded seize upon terrible suffering
through causing suffering to each other.
Whatever calamities there are in the world,
whatever sufferings and fears —
all of them arise from clinging to the self.
What then is the use of this clinging of mine?
Without abandoning the self,
suffering cannot be abandoned —
just as without abandoning fire,
burning cannot be abandoned.
Therefore, for the pacification of my own suffering
and for the calming of the suffering of others,
I give myself to others
and adopt others as myself.
'I am bound to another' —
make this resolution firm, O my mind!
Having set aside everything for the sake of all beings,
you should think of nothing else now.
It is not right, with eyes belonging to them,
to see for one's own benefit.
It is not right to use hands belonging to others
to accomplish one's own purpose.
Therefore, having become devoted to beings,
whatever you see in this body,
seize that very thing from it
and use it for the benefit of others.
Having made oneself into the inferior and the like,
and also [making] the other into oneself,
meditate on envy and pride
with a mind free from conceptual elaboration.
This one is honored, not I;
this one gains, not I, as he does.
This one is praised, I am blamed;
I am suffering, he is happy.
I do the work,
while this one sits at ease.
This one is said to be great in the world;
I am said to be lowly and without qualities.
What is to be done with one who has no qualities?
Everyone has a self endowed with qualities.
There are those before whom I am inferior;
there are those before whom I am superior.
The decline in morality, views, and the like
is due to the power of the afflictions, not under my control.
I should be treated as best one can;
I accept even the pain [of treatment].
But if I am incurable by him,
why does he disparage me?
What use are his qualities to me?
He is the one who has qualities.
He has no compassion for people
who are in the jaws of beasts of bad destinations;
[yet] through pride in his qualities,
he wishes to outdo the wise.
Seeing himself as equal [to another],
for the growth of his own superiority,
he would procure gain and honor for himself
even through quarrel.
Would that my qualities
be made manifest everywhere in the world,
and would that whatever qualities he has
may no one hear of at all.
Would that my faults be concealed,
and would that I be worshipped and he not.
My gains are well obtained today;
I am honored, but he is not.
Let us watch with joy
as he is at last put to shame,
becoming the laughingstock of all people,
being blamed here and there.
This wretched one also
apparently competes with me!
Is his learning, wisdom, beauty,
family, or wealth equal to mine?
Thus, hearing my own qualities
being proclaimed here and there,
with hair standing on end and overjoyed,
I shall enjoy a festival of happiness.
Even if he should have gain,
it should be seized by us by force.
Giving him only bare sustenance,
if he works for us.
He should be dislodged from happiness
and always yoked to our suffering.
Through this one [i.e., self-cherishing], all of us
have been tormented in <s>saṃsāra</s> hundreds of times.
Immeasurable aeons have passed
while you, [O mind], sought your own interest.
Through this great exertion,
you have earned only suffering.
At my urging, here too,
engage without hesitation.
You will see the advantages of this later,
for the word of the Sage is true.
Had this practice been done
by you before,
this state would not have come about,
separated from the perfect happiness of <s>Buddhahood</s>.
Therefore, just as you have made
the notion of 'I' in another's
drops of semen and blood,
cultivate it likewise in others too.
Having become a spy for others,
whatever you see in this body,
seize that very thing
and use it for the benefit of others.
This one is well-off, the other suffers;
this one is high, the other low.
The other acts, this one does not —
cultivate envy toward yourself.
Dislodge yourself from happiness
and assign yourself to the suffering of others.
'When does this one do what?' —
examine the deceit of this one [i.e., the self].
Even a fault committed by another
should be made to fall upon this one's head.
And even a small fault of this one
should be disclosed before the Great Sage.
By proclaiming the greater fame of another,
sully the reputation of this one.
And like the lowest servant,
set him to work in the tasks of beings.
This one, who is full of faults,
is not to be praised for some adventitious quality.
Act so that no one may know
any quality of his.
In short, whatever harm
you have done to others for your own sake,
let that very harm fall upon yourself
for the sake of beings.
He should not be given the boldness
by which he would become loquacious.
He should be kept in the manner of a new bride —
modest, fearful, and restrained.
Do thus! Stay thus!
This must not be done by you!
Thus he should be brought under control
and disciplined when he transgresses.
And if, even when told thus,
O mind, you will not do this,
I shall restrain you yourself,
for all faults depend on you.
Where will you go? I see you.
I shall crush all your pride.
That former time was different,
when you had destroyed me.
'I still have my own interest' —
abandon this hope now!
You have been sold by me to others,
without thinking of the many hardships.
If through heedlessness I do not
give you over to beings,
you will certainly deliver me
to the wardens of hell.
Thus, having given [me] over many times,
you have tormented me for long.
Remembering those enmities,
I shall destroy you, O slave of self-interest.
If you take delight in yourself,
you should not take delight in yourself.
If the self is to be protected,
it is not proper to protect [it in this way].
The more this body
is pampered and nurtured,
the more delicate it becomes,
and the more it falls [into ruin].
And when it has fallen thus,
even this entire earth
is not enough to fulfill its desire.
Then who will fulfill its wish?
For one who desires the impossible,
affliction and disappointment arise.
But for one who is without expectation in all things,
prosperity is inexhaustible.
Therefore, the body should not be given scope
for the growth of its desires.
That thing is truly good
which is not grasped at because it is desirable.
This [body], whose end is in ashes,
which is inert, moved by another,
a terrifying statue of impurity —
why is there my attachment to it?
What is this machine to me,
whether alive or dead?
How does it differ from a clod of earth?
Alas, the sense of 'I' does not perish!
Through partiality for the body,
suffering is uselessly accumulated.
What use is aversion or affection
toward this thing that is like a piece of wood?
Whether nurtured by me thus
or eaten by vultures and the like —

Why then do I love it?
If [the body itself] does not know anger from abuse
or pleasure from worship,
for whose sake then
is this exertion of mine?
Those who like this body,
they too are said to be my friends.
But all like their own bodies —
why then are they not dear to me [as well]?
Therefore, without attachment, the body
has been given up by me for the welfare of the world.
Hence, though it has many faults,
it is maintained as a vessel for action.
Enough of worldly ways!
I shall follow the wise,

Therefore, to destroy the obstructions,

Chapter 9
All this preparation
was taught by the Sage for the sake of wisdom.
Therefore, one should generate wisdom,
with the aspiration to end suffering.
<s>Saṃvṛti</s> (conventional [truth]) and <s>paramārtha</s> (ultimate [truth]) —
these two truths are accepted.
Reality is beyond the range of the intellect;
the intellect is called <s>saṃvṛti</s> (the concealing one).
Therein, the world is seen as twofold:
the <s>yogin</s> and the ordinary person.
There, the world of the ordinary person
is superseded by the world of the <s>yogin</s>.
Even <s>yogins</s> are superseded
by successively higher ones, through distinctions of understanding,
by means of examples accepted by both parties,
for a practical purpose, without [ultimate] analysis.
Things are seen by the world
and are also imagined to be real.
But not as being like an illusion — and herein lies
the dispute between the <s>yogin</s> and the world.
Even form and the like, [known by] direct perception,
are [established] by convention, not by valid cognition.
That convention is false,
like the convention [that sees] purity in what is impure.
For the purpose of guiding the world,
entities were taught by the Protector.
In reality, these are not momentary —
if [it is said they are so only] conventionally, there is a contradiction.
There is no fault from the <s>yogin</s>'s conventional [standpoint],
since he is a seer of reality compared to the world.
Otherwise, the world would be contradicted
in the examination of a woman as impure.
How does merit arise from a <s>Jina</s> who is like an illusion,
even if he really exists?
If a being is like an illusion,
how then is he reborn after dying?
As long as the assemblage of conditions [persists],
even an illusion persists.
How is a being truly real
merely through a long continuum?
In the killing of an illusory person and the like,
there is no sin, because there is no mind.
The mind-[created] magical illusion arises
from both sin and merit.
Due to the incapacity of mantras and the like,
the magical illusion does not arise from the mind [of the magician alone];
that magical illusion too is of various kinds,
arising from various conditions.
No single condition has the power
to produce everything.
If one who is ultimately liberated (<s>nirvṛta</s>)
would still transmigrate conventionally,
then even a <s>Buddha</s> would transmigrate;
and then what use is the <s>bodhisattva</s>'s practice?
For as long as the conditions are not cut off,
even the magical illusion is not cut off.
But when the conditions are severed,
even conventionally, it does not arise.
When there is not even the delusion,
by whom is the illusion perceived?
When the illusion itself does not exist for you,
then what is perceived?
It is merely an aspect of the mind,
even though in reality it is something other.
If the mind itself is the illusion,
then what is seen by what?
The Protector of the World has said:
'The mind does not see the mind.'
Just as a sword-blade cannot
cut itself, so too the mind.
'But the lamp illuminates
its own nature' — if so objected,
the lamp is not itself illuminated,
because it is not covered by darkness.
Unlike a crystal, blue[ness]
does not depend on another [to appear] blue.
Similarly, something is seen as dependent on another
and [something else] as independent.
When it is not blue, it cannot make
itself blue by itself.
For who could make what is already blue
become blue by itself?
When it is not blue, it cannot make
itself blue by itself.
'The lamp illuminates' — this is said
knowing it through knowledge;
'The mind illuminates' — this being known,
by what is it said?
Whether luminous or not luminous,
when it is seen by no one,
like the charm of a barren woman's daughter,
speaking of it is pointless.
If there is no self-awareness (<s>svasaṃvitti</s>),
how is consciousness remembered?
Memory arises from the connection with the experience of another [object],
like the rat-poison [remembered when the effect appears later].
When endowed with other conditions,
it illuminates itself, [you say];
[but] what is seen through the application of magic eye-ointment
is the pot, not the ointment itself.
What is seen, heard, or known
is not denied here;
but the mental fabrication of [it as] real,
which is the cause of suffering, is what is prevented.
If the illusion is not other than the mind,
it should not be conceived as non-other either;
if it is a real thing, how can it not be other?
And if other, it does not truly exist.
Just as the illusion, though unreal,
can be seen, so too the mind is the seer.
If <s>saṃsāra</s> has a real substratum,
then it would be other, like space.
How can a non-existent thing
have efficacy through a real substratum?
For in your view, the mind becomes
something accompanied by what is unreal, and alone.
When the mind is freed from the grasped [object],
then all [beings] are <s>Tathāgatas</s>;
if so, then what virtue is gained
by positing mind-only?
Even when the similarity to illusion is known,
how do afflictions cease?
For even the creator of the magical woman
can develop desire for her.
Indeed, the creator's latent tendencies
toward affliction regarding the knowable have not been abandoned;
therefore, at the time of seeing her,
his tendency toward emptiness is weak.
Through cultivation of the tendency toward emptiness,
the tendency toward [real] existence is abandoned;
and through the practice of 'nothing exists at all,'
even that [tendency toward emptiness] is later abandoned.
When no entity can be found
that is conceived as 'nonexistent,'
then non-existence, being without a basis,
how can it remain before the mind?
When neither existence nor non-existence
remains before the mind,
then, there being no other alternative,
the mind, without support, is pacified.
Just as the wish-fulfilling gem and the wish-fulfilling tree
fulfill all wishes,
so the image of the <s>Jina</s> is seen
through [his] disciples and [his] vow.
Just as the <s>Gāruḍika</s> (snake-charmer), having consecrated a pillar,
passes away,
yet that [pillar], even long after his death,
still neutralizes poisons and the like;
so too, the pillar of the <s>Jina</s>,
consecrated in accordance with the <s>bodhisattva</s>'s practice,
accomplishes all purposes
even when the <s>bodhisattva</s> has passed into <s>nirvāṇa</s>.
'How can worship offered to something without mind
bear fruit?'
Because it is taught as equal,
whether he is present or in <s>nirvāṇa</s>.
And from scripture, there is fruit in that [worship],
whether conventionally or ultimately;
just as worship offered to the real <s>Buddha</s>
is fruitful — so [it is here].
'Liberation comes from seeing the truth;
so what is the use of seeing emptiness?'
Because the scriptures state that
without this path there is no awakening.
'But the <s>Mahāyāna</s> is not established [as authentic]!'
How then is your scripture established?
'Because it is accepted by both.'
But it was not accepted by you at the start.
Whatever reasons ground your faith in that [your scripture],
apply those to the <s>Mahāyāna</s> as well.
If something is true because accepted by two parties,
then the <s>Vedas</s> and the like would also be true.
'The <s>Mahāyāna</s> is disputed' —
if so, then abandon your own scripture too,
since it is disputed by non-Buddhists;
and other scriptures [are disputed] by both your own and others.
The teaching has monasticism as its root,
and monasticism itself is difficult;
for those whose minds still have a support [i.e., object],
even <s>nirvāṇa</s> is difficult to sustain.
'If liberation comes from abandoning afflictions,
let it come immediately after [that abandonment].'
Yet there is observed in them the power
of action [even] without afflictions.
'Craving as grasping (<s>upādāna</s>)
does not exist [in them]' — if that is your position,
why should unafflicted craving not exist in them
as it exists [in the form of] delusion?
Craving arises from the condition of feeling,
and feeling exists in them;
the mind with a support [i.e., an object]
must abide somewhere.
Without emptiness, the mind,
though bound, arises again,
as in the attainment of cessation;
therefore one should meditate on emptiness.
If whatever statement appears in a <s>sūtra</s>
is accepted as the <s>Buddha</s>'s word,
then the <s>Mahāyāna</s> is mostly similar to your <s>sūtras</s> —
why is it not accepted?
If, because one [text] is not accepted [by you],
the whole is defective,
then, because one [text] is similar to [your] <s>sūtras</s>,
why is not everything the word of the <s>Jina</s>?
That whose words could not be fathomed
even by those headed by <s>Mahākāśyapa</s> —
who will disregard it
because it is not understood by you?
Through attachment, fear of liberation [from self],
remaining in <s>saṃsāra</s> is accomplished;
through delusion, for the sake of suffering beings —
this is the fruit of emptiness.
Therefore, objections against the position
of emptiness are not valid;
therefore, without hesitation,
emptiness is to be meditated upon.
Emptiness is the antidote to the darkness
of the obscurations of afflictions and of the knowable;
how can one who desires omniscience quickly
not meditate upon it?
Let fear arise
toward that which produces suffering;
emptiness pacifies suffering —
why then should fear arise from it?
Let fear come from whatever source,
if there is something called 'I';
but if the 'I' itself is nothing,
whose fear will there be?
I am not the teeth, the hair, or the nails;
I am not the bones, nor am I the blood;
I am not the nasal mucus, nor the phlegm;
I am not the pus, nor the lymph.
I am not the fat, nor the sweat;
the membrane and the entrails are not I either;
nor am I the inner tissue of the intestines;
I am not the excrement or the urine.
I am not the flesh, nor the sinews;
I am not heat, nor am I the wind;
I am not the orifices, nor am I
the six consciousnesses in any way.
If the knowledge of sound [were the self],
then sound would always be apprehended;
but without an object to be known, what does it know,
by which it is designated as 'knowledge'?
If knowledge were unknowing,
then a piece of wood would be knowledge;
therefore, in the absence of a proximate object,
it is certain that knowledge does not exist.
If that [consciousness] itself knows form,
then why does it not also hear?
'Because of the absence of sound' —
then the knowledge of that [sound] also does not exist.
How can that which has the nature of apprehending sound
be the apprehension of form?
One [person] is conceived as both father and son,
but not in reality.
Since <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s>
are neither son nor father,
its nature as conjoined with the apprehension of sound
is not observed [when apprehending form].
It is the same [consciousness] in another form,
like an actor — yet it too is impermanent;
if it is the same yet of a different nature,
then this unity is unprecedented.
If the other form is unreal,
then let its own true form be stated;
if it is knowingness — then the unity
of all persons would follow.
There would also be unity of the conscious and the non-conscious,
since both equally have existence;
and when the differentia are false,
what then is the basis for similarity?
And [the self posited as] non-conscious is not the 'I,'
because it lacks consciousness, like a cloth and the like;
but if it knows through conjunction with consciousness,
then it follows that the unknowing [self] has perished.
But if the self is unchanging,
then what has consciousness done for it?
Thus the self — unknowing, inactive —
is deemed [equivalent to] the selfhood of space.
'But without a self, the connection
of action and fruit would not be proper;
for when the action is done and has perished,
whose fruit will it be?'
Since both of us agree
that action and fruit have different substrata,
and the self has no role there —
is this debate not pointless?
'One endowed with the cause is endowed with the fruit' —
this [connection] is not observed [as requiring a self];
relying on the unity of the mental continuum,
agent and experiencer are taught.
The past or future mind is not 'I,'
for that does not exist;
if the presently arisen mind were 'I,'
then when it perishes, the 'I' no longer exists.
Just as the trunk of a plantain tree
is nothing when split into parts,
so too the 'I,' when sought
through analysis, is found to be non-existent.
'If no being exists,
toward whom is there compassion?' — if so asked,
[it is toward] whoever is projected through delusion,
accepted for the sake of the task [of liberation].
'Whose task is it, if there is no being?'
True, the effort [itself] is from delusion;
but for the purpose of the cessation of suffering,
the delusion of [positing] the task is not prevented.
The ego-grasping, which is the cause of suffering,
increases through the delusion of self;
'If even that cannot be averted' —
then the meditation on selflessness is better.
The body is not the feet, nor the shins;
the body is not the thighs, nor the waist;
it is not the belly, nor the back;
it is not the chest, nor the arms.
It is not the hands, nor the sides;
it is not the armpits, nor defined by the shoulders;
it is not the neck, nor the head;
then what here is the body?
If the body exists partially
in all of these parts,
the parts exist in [their own] parts —
where does the body itself reside?
If the body exists in its entirety
in the hands and the like,
then there would be as many bodies
as there are hands and the like.
The body is neither inside nor outside;
how then is the body in the hands and the like?
It does not exist apart from the hands and the like —
how then can it exist at all?
Therefore the body does not exist; but through delusion
the notion of 'body' [arises] with regard to the hands and the like,
on account of a particular arrangement,
as the notion of 'person' [arises with regard] to a post.
As long as the assemblage of conditions [exists],
so long the body [appears], like a person [in a post];
likewise, as long as [the conditions] exist in the hands and the like,
so long the body is seen in them.
Similarly, since it is a collection of toes,
what would the foot be?
The toe too, being a collection of joints —
and the joint too, through the division of its own parts.
The parts too, through the division into atoms;
and the atom too, through the division into directions;
and the directional part, being without parts,
is like space; therefore the atom does not exist.
Thus, what discerning person would be attached
to form, which is like a dream?
When the body does not exist in this way,
then what is woman? And what is man?
If suffering exists in reality,
why does it not torment the joyful?
If delicious food and the like are [real] happiness,
why do they not please one afflicted by grief?
'It is not experienced because it is overpowered
by something stronger' — but if so,
how can that which is not of the nature of experience
be a feeling?
'Suffering exists in subtle form,
its gross aspect having been removed' —
if the other [i.e., pleasure] is merely a lesser [form of suffering],
then that [pleasure] too is its subtle form.
If suffering does not arise
when its contrary condition is produced,
then it follows that what is called 'feeling'
is merely a conceptual superimposition.
For this very reason, this analysis
should be cultivated as its antidote;
for the food of <s>yogins</s> is meditation,
arising from the field of conceptualization.
If there is a gap between the sense and the object,
how can the two come into contact?
And if there is no gap — they would be one;
what then would come into contact with what?
There is no penetration of one atom into another,
for it is without interstice and is equal [in size];
without penetration there is no mingling;
without mingling there is no contact.
How indeed can there be contact
of something that has no parts?
And if partlessness in contact
has been observed — show the example!
Contact with consciousness, which is immaterial,
is simply not possible;
nor [is contact possible] with an aggregate, because it has no [real] existence,
as was previously analyzed.
Thus, in the absence of contact,
how can feeling arise?
For what purpose is this exertion?
To whom could harm come, and from where?
When there is no one who feels
and feeling too does not exist,
then, seeing this state of things,
O craving, why do you not fall apart?
What is seen and what is touched
is of a dream-like, illusion-like nature;
since feeling arises simultaneously with the mind,
it is not perceived by it.
What arises earlier or later
is remembered, not [directly] experienced;
it does not experience itself,
nor is it experienced by another.
There is no one who feels;
therefore feeling does not really exist.
in this selfless aggregate,
who indeed is harmed by it?
Not in the sense-organs, not in form and the like,
not in the space between does the mind abide;
neither within nor without is consciousness [found],
nor is it found anywhere else.
That which is neither in the body nor elsewhere,
neither mixed nor separate anywhere —
that is nothing at all; therefore beings
are by nature in <s>nirvāṇa</s>.
If knowledge exists prior to the knowable,
depending on what does it arise?
If knowledge [arises] simultaneously with the knowable,
depending on what does it arise?
And if it arises after the knowable,
then from where would knowledge arise?
Thus, the origination of all <s>dharmas</s>
cannot be established.
If so, conventional [truth] does not exist;
then how can there be the two truths?
If [conventional truth] exists by another's convention,
how could a being [ever] attain <s>nirvāṇa</s>?
That [conventional truth] is a conceptual construct of another's mind;
by one's own convention, it does not exist.
If it is later established, then it exists;
if not, convention itself does not exist.
The conceptualization and the conceptualized —
the two depend on each other.
All analysis is expressed
in dependence on what is commonly accepted.
But when the analysis itself
is analyzed by analysis,
then there is an infinite regress,
since that analysis too would be analyzed.
But when the object of analysis is analyzed,
the analysis has no basis;
because it has no basis, it does not arise —
and that is called <s>nirvāṇa</s>.
But for one who holds both [knowledge and object] to be real,
he is in an extremely difficult position.
If the object depends on knowledge,
what basis is there for the existence of knowledge?
And if knowledge depends on the knowable,
what basis is there for the existence of the knowable?
If their existence depends on each other,
then both would be non-existent.
If there is no father without a son,
how does the son come into being?
In the absence of a son, there is no father —
likewise, the existence of those two [knowledge and object].
A sprout arises from a seed,
and by that very [sprout] the seed is indicated.
By the knowledge arisen from the knowable,
why is the existence of that [knowable] not understood?
From knowledge other than the sprout,
the existence of the seed is understood.
From what is the existence of that knowledge understood
by which the knowable is apprehended?
The world, by direct perception,
observes that everything has a cause;
for the differentiation of lotus stalks and the like
arises from the differentiation of causes.
If you ask, 'What produced the differentiation of causes?' —
[it comes] from the differentiation of prior causes.
And why does a cause give its fruit?
By the power of prior causes.
If <s>Īśvara</s> (God) is the cause of the world,
say — what then is <s>Īśvara</s>?
If [you say] 'the elements' — let it be so;
why then the trouble over a mere name?
Moreover, [the elements] are many, impermanent,
inert, and not divine;
they can be stepped upon and are impure —
earth and the like are not that <s>Īśvara</s>.
Space is not the Lord, being inert;
not the self, as that was refuted before.
And the authorship of the inconceivable —
what can be said about what is itself inconceivable?
And what does He wish to create?
If the self — is not that eternal?
The nature of earth and the like, and <s>Īśvara</s>,
and knowledge from the knowable — [are all] beginningless.
Happiness and suffering come from <s>karma</s>;
tell me — what then did He create?
If the cause has no beginning,
how could the effect have a beginning?
Why does He not always create?
For He does not depend on anything else.
There is nothing else not made by Him;
so what would He depend upon?
If He depends on an assemblage [of conditions],
He is no longer the cause — <s>Īśvara</s> is not.
He cannot refrain from creating when the assemblage is present,
nor can He create in its absence.
If <s>Īśvara</s> creates without wishing to,
it follows He is dependent on another.
Even if He wishes, He would depend on desire;
where then is the lordship of one who creates [under compulsion]?
Those who speak of eternal atoms —
they too were refuted before.
The <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> posit <s>Pradhāna</s>
as the eternal cause of the world.
<s>Sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s> —
the <s>guṇas</s> in a state of equilibrium —
are called <s>Pradhāna</s>;
the world is said [to arise] from their imbalance.
That a single thing should have a triple nature
is illogical; therefore it does not exist.
Likewise, the <s>guṇas</s> do not exist,
since each of them too is threefold.
In the absence of the <s>guṇas</s>,
the existence of sound and the like is extremely remote;
and in non-conscious things like cloth and the like,
pleasure and the like are also impossible.
If [you say] things have the form of those causes —
have not things been [already] analyzed?
Moreover, your cause is pleasure and the like;
but cloth and the like do not [arise] from that.
Pleasure and the like may arise from cloth and the like,
but in their absence, pleasure and the like are unreal.
And the permanence of pleasure and the like
is never observed.
If pleasure exists manifestly,
why is its apprehension not perceived?
If [you say] it becomes subtle —
how can it be both gross and subtle?
Having abandoned grossness, it becomes subtle —
grossness and subtlety would be impermanent.
Why then do you not accept
the impermanence of all things in the same way?
If grossness is not other than pleasure,
then the impermanence of pleasure is evident.
'Nothing arises from what is non-existent
because of its non-existence' — if such is your view,
the arising of the manifest from the non-existent
is established even against your will.
One who eats food would be eating filth,
if the fruit exists [already] in the cause.
Then buy cotton seeds with the price of cloth
and wear them.
If [you say] the world does not perceive this due to delusion,
that same condition holds for the knower of truth.
The world too has that knowledge —
why does it not perceive [the effect in the cause]?
If [you say] the world is not a valid authority,
then even its perception of the manifest is invalid.
If the [world's] means of knowledge is not a valid means —
then what it cognizes is false;
therefore, the emptiness of things
in reality would not be established.
Without encountering the imputed thing,
its non-existence cannot be apprehended.
Therefore, whatever thing is false,
its non-existence is clearly [also] false.
Thus, when in a dream one's son has died,
the thought 'he does not exist'
obstructs the arising of the thought of his existence —
and it too is false.
Therefore, through such analysis,
nothing exists without a cause;
nor does it abide in conditions
either severally or collectively.
It has not come from elsewhere;
it neither abides nor departs.
What difference is there from an illusion
in that which the deluded take to be real?
That which is created by illusion
and that which is created by causes —
examine: from where does it come
and where does it go?
That which is seen through the proximity of another
and [disappears] in its absence —
being like a reflection,
how can it be real, being artificial?
For a thing that already exists,
what need is there for a cause?
And if it is non-existent,
what need, again, for a cause?
Non-existence is not transformed
even by hundreds of millions of causes.
How can what is in that state become an existent?
And what else could attain existence?
If there is no existent at the time of non-existence,
when will the existent come to be?
For that non-existence will not depart
until the existent has been produced.
And while non-existence has not departed,
there is no occasion for existence;
nor does an existent pass into non-existence,
for that would entail a dual nature.
Thus there is neither destruction
nor existence at any time.
This entire world is therefore
unborn and unceased.
The states [of existence] are like a dream;
upon analysis, they are like a plantain tree.
Between those in <s>nirvāṇa</s> and those not in <s>nirvāṇa</s>,
there is no difference in reality.
When all <s>dharmas</s> are thus empty,
what can be gained, what can be lost?
Who will be honored or despised
by whom?
From where [comes] pleasure or pain?
What is pleasant or unpleasant?
What craving, and where is that craving
when sought for in its own nature?
Upon analysis, what is the world of the living?
Who here will die?
Who will come to be? Who has been?
Who is a relative? Who is a friend of whom?
Let those like me understand
that everything is like space.
They become angry and elated
through causes of quarrel and festivity.
Through grief, toil, and despair,
through mutual cutting and wounding,
they pass their lives with great difficulty
through sins, desiring their own happiness.
They die and fall into lower realms
of long and intense suffering,
and returning again and again to the happy states,
becoming accustomed again and again to pleasure.
In existence there are many precipices,
and therein the reality is not like this [emptiness];
there is mutual contradiction —
the reality cannot be like this.
There are incomparable, intense,
infinite oceans of suffering;
there is scanty strength,
and there is the brevity of life.
There too, in pursuits for livelihood and health,
in hunger, fatigue, and exertion,
in sleep, in calamities, and in fruitless
association with fools,
life passes swiftly and in vain;
and discernment is so hard to find.
There too, where can one find the means
to avert habitual distraction?
There too, <s>Māra</s> strives
to cast [beings] into the great precipice of lower realms.
There, because of the abundance of wrong paths,
doubt is hard to overcome.
Moreover, a [human] rebirth is extremely rare,
the arising of a <s>Buddha</s> is most difficult to obtain,
and the flood of afflictions is hard to restrain —
alas, what a succession of sufferings!
Alas, how greatly to be pitied
are these beings caught in the flood of suffering,
who do not see their own wretched state,
even though they are so extremely wretched.
Just as someone who bathes again and again
enters fire again and again,
and yet considers themselves to be well —
even though they are so extremely wretched.
Those who live as though they were not subject
to aging and death, acting thus —
terrible misfortunes shall befall them,
with death at the forefront.
When shall I bring peace
to those scorched by the fire of suffering,
with my own provisions of happiness
arisen from the clouds of merit?
When shall I teach emptiness
to those with views of apprehension,
while earnestly accumulating the store of merit
through convention, by means of non-apprehension?
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Perfection of Wisdom (<s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>), in the <s>Bodhicaryāvatāra</s>. |
Chapter 10
Whatever merit has arisen from
my contemplating the <s>Bodhicaryāvatāra</s> —
by that, may all people
become adorned with the conduct of awakening.
In all directions, as many as there are
beings afflicted with bodily and mental suffering —
may they, through my merits,
obtain oceans of happiness and joy.
May their happiness never diminish
as long as <s>saṃsāra</s> lasts;
may the world without interruption
attain the happiness of the <s>Bodhisattvas</s>.
Whatever hells exist
in the world-systems —
may the beings therein rejoice
in the delights and joys of <s>Sukhāvatī</s>.
May those afflicted by cold find warmth;
may those afflicted by heat be cooled
by oceans of water born from
the great clouds of the <s>Bodhisattvas</s>.
May the sword-leaf forests become for them
the splendor of the <s>Nandana</s> garden;
may the thorny <s>śālmalī</s> trees
become wish-fulfilling trees.
May the regions of hell become delightful
with lakes lovely with the fragrance of full-blown lotuses,
charming with the cries of <s>dātyūha</s> birds, <s>kāraṇḍava</s> ducks,
<s>cakravāka</s> geese, swans, and the like.
May that heap of embers become a heap of gems;
may the burning ground become a crystal pavement;
may the crushing mountains become
celestial mansions of worship, filled with <s>Sugatas</s>.
May the rain of embers, heated stones, and weapons
from this day forth become a rain of flowers;
may the mutual fighting with weapons
from today become a playful flower-fight.
May those whose flesh has completely fallen off, whose bodies are bone-white,
submerged in the <s>Vaitaraṇī</s> river whose waters are like blazing fire —
through the power of my merit, having attained divine bodies,
abide at the <s>Mandākinī</s> river together with celestial maidens.
Let them look and wonder: 'Why are <s>Yama</s>'s servants and the dreadful crows and vultures suddenly terrified here?

children.text: dṛṣṭvā prāmodyavegād vyapagataduritā yāṃtu tenaiva sārdham

seen to extinguish the fires of hell — 'Peace!'
'What is this?' — suffused with happiness and wonder —

children.translated_text: 'Come, come quickly! Cast off fear! Brothers, we are alive!

by whose power all misfortune has vanished and torrents of joy have begun to flow;

'Behold him — his lotus-feet worshipped by the crowns of hundreds of gods,
his gaze moist with compassion, a rain of manifold flowers falling on his head,
celebrated by thousands of goddesses in delightful mansions resounding with praise —'

children.text: dṛṣṭvāgre mañjughoṣaṃ bhavatu kalakalaḥ sāṃprataṃ nārakāṇām
children.translated_text: beholding <s>Mañjughoṣa</s> before them, may there be a tumult of joy among the hell-beings.
Thus, by my merits, beholding the unobstructed
<s>Bodhisattva</s>-clouds headed by <s>Samantabhadra</s>,
raining pleasant, cool, fragrant breezes and showers —
may those hell-beings rejoice.
May the intense sufferings of the hell-beings
and their fears be pacified.
May all who dwell in lower realms
be freed from the lower realms.
May the fear of devouring one another
depart from the animals.
May the hungry ghosts be happy
like the people of <s>Uttarakuru</s>.

children.translated_text: May the hungry ghosts be satiated, bathed, and always cooled by the streams of milk flowing from the hand of noble <s>Avalokiteśvara</s>. ||
May the blind see forms;
may the deaf hear at all times.
May pregnant women give birth
without pain, like <s>Māyādevī</s>.
May they obtain clothing, food, drink,
garlands, sandalwood, and ornaments —
everything the mind desires,
that is conducive to their welfare.
May the frightened be freed from fear;
may those afflicted with grief find joy.
May the anxious be free from anxiety
and become resolute.
May the sick have health;
may all be freed from every bondage.
May the weak become strong,
their hearts affectionate toward one another.
May all directions be auspicious
for all who travel the roads.
Whatever purpose they go for,
may it be accomplished by the [proper] means.
May those who travel by boat or vehicle
have their wishes fulfilled.
Having safely reached the shore,
may they rejoice with their relatives.
May those who have fallen off the road in the wilderness
find a caravan-company.
May they travel without weariness,
free from the fear of robbers, tigers, and the like.
For those asleep, intoxicated, or heedless,
in the dangers of illness, forests, and the like —
for the helpless, the young, and the old —
may the gods provide protection.
May all be freed from every unfavorable condition,
endowed with faith, wisdom, and compassion,
perfect in form and conduct,
and always remember their former lives.
May their treasuries be inexhaustible,
like [the treasure of] <s>Naganagañja</s>.
Free from conflict, without intrigue,
may they be self-governing in their livelihood.
May beings of little strength
become beings of great strength.
May the deformed and wretched
become endowed with beauty.
Whatever women there are in the world,
may they attain manhood.
May the lowly attain high status,
and may their pride be destroyed.
By this merit of mine,
may all beings without exception,
having ceased from all sins,
always practice what is wholesome.
Never separated from the mind of awakening (<s>bodhicitta</s>),
devoted to the practice of awakening,
accepted by the <s>Buddhas</s>,
and free from the deeds of <s>Māra</s> —
may all those beings
have immeasurable lifespans.
May they live always in happiness,
and may even the word 'death' perish.
May all directions become delightful
with gardens of wish-fulfilling trees,
filled with <s>Buddhas</s> and sons of <s>Buddhas</s>,
with the enchanting sound of the <s>Dharma</s>.
Free from pebbles and the like,
level, like the surface of a palm,
soft, and made of lapis lazuli —
may the earth everywhere be thus.
May the great assemblies of <s>Bodhisattvas</s>
sit in circles all around,
adorning the surface of the earth
with their own splendor.
From the birds, from all the trees,
from the rays of light, and from the sky itself,
may the sound of the <s>Dharma</s> be heard unceasingly
by all embodied beings.
May they always encounter
<s>Buddhas</s> and sons of <s>Buddhas</s>.
May they worship the teacher of the world
with boundless clouds of offerings.
May the rains fall in due season;
may there be abundance of crops.
May the world prosper,
and may the king be righteous.
May medicines be potent;
may the mantras of those who recite them be efficacious.
May <s>ḍākinīs</s>, <s>rākṣasas</s>, and others
become filled with compassion.
May no being be unhappy,
may none be sinful, may none be ill.
May none be despised or lowly,
and may no one be dejected.
May monasteries be well-established,
resounding with recitation and study.
May the <s>Saṃgha</s> always be in harmony,
and may the purpose of the <s>Saṃgha</s> be accomplished.
May monks who desire training
attain solitude.
May they meditate with minds ready for practice,
free from all distraction.
May nuns receive provisions,
free from quarrel and hardship.
May all who have gone forth
maintain their moral conduct unbroken.
May those of poor conduct feel remorse
and always delight in the exhaustion of sin.
May they attain [rebirth] with the <s>Sugatas</s>,
and there maintain their vows unbroken.
May the wise be honored,
may those who beg for alms receive provisions.
May their continua of mind be pure,
and their fame spread in all directions.
Without suffering the pains of the lower realms,
without difficult austerities,
with a single divine body
may the world attain Buddhahood.
May all the perfectly awakened ones
be worshipped by all beings in manifold ways.
May they be happy exceedingly
with the inconceivable bliss of a <s>Buddha</s>.
May the wishes of the <s>Bodhisattvas</s>
for the welfare of the world be fulfilled.
Whatever those protectors intend,
may it be accomplished for all beings.
May the <s>Pratyekabuddhas</s> and the <s>Śrāvakas</s>
be happy likewise,
always worshipped with respect
by gods, <s>asuras</s>, and humans.
May I always attain
the memory of former lives and the going forth,
until the Joyful Stage [first <s>bhūmi</s>],
through the grace of <s>Mañjughoṣa</s>.
In whatever posture I may live,
may I be endowed with strength.
May I attain the conditions for dwelling in solitude
in all my births.
And whenever I wish to see
or ask about anything,
may I behold that very protector,
the Lord <s>Mañjunātha</s>, without hindrance.
As <s>Mañjuśrī</s> acts
to accomplish the welfare of all beings
to the ends of the sky in all ten directions —
may my conduct be the same.
As long as space endures,
and as long as the world endures,
may I endure as well,
destroying the sufferings of the world.
Whatever suffering there is in the world,
may it all ripen upon me.
And through the virtues of the <s>Bodhisattvas</s>,
may the world be made happy.
May the Teaching — the sole medicine
for the suffering of the world, the source
of all prosperity and happiness —
endure long, with honor and support.
I bow to <s>Mañjughoṣa</s>,
by whose grace my mind turns to virtue.
I salute my spiritual friend,
by whose grace [virtue] also increases.
[End of] the tenth chapter, the Dedication (<s>Pariṇāmanā</s>), in the <s>Bodhicaryāvatāra</s>. ||
